na8da204bfec1: Terraces play a vital role in mitigating runoff and intercepting sediment. Large-scale, high-precision extraction of terraces from remote sensing imagery is essential for environmental monitoring and soil erosion control. However, accurate spatial identification of terraces still presents significant challenges, including scale variability, shadow interference, and complex geometric configurations. To address these issues, we propose DETS-Net, a dual-encoder network that integrates CNN and Transformer architectures. The network employs ResNet-34 as the CNN encoder for local feature detail extraction, utilizes a Transformer encoder to strengthen long-range dependency modeling, and incorporates an adaptive feature fusion (AFF) module for the dynamic integration of the two feature branches. We develop the THDIR dataset, which covers four typical terrain types, namely, plateau mountains, hills, and mountain-basin transition zones, and contains 9,336 standardized 256 × 256 pixel images. We conduct systematic comparisons with eight representative deep learning models. Experimental results demonstrate that DETS-Net achieves an overall accuracy (OA) of 89.91%, a mean intersection over union (MIoU) of 81.28%, and an F1-score of 87.99% on the THDIR dataset, outperforming current mainstream methods in segmentation precision. We apply the optimized model to 2023 remote sensing imagery of Luotian County in the Dabie Mountains, Hubei Province, and generate a high-precision county-level terrace spatial distribution map. This framework supports the assessment of soil and water conservation benefits through area statistics, slope distribution data, and high-precision boundary extraction and provides a reproducible technical pathway for automated terrace mapping using high-resolution remote sensing imagery in complex mountainous regions.
n426eea67c084: Freshwater salinization and alkalization are emerging threats to global biodiversity, particularly in arid and semi-arid regions. Although ecological impacts of freshwater salinization and alkalization on local biodiversity have received increasing attention, it remains unclear how diversity patterns of organisms in different trophic levels respond at a regional scale. Here, we investigated rotifer and phytoplankton assemblages across 61 wetlands spanning a broad saline–alkaline gradient in the Songnen Plain, Northeast China. We quantified local (alpha) diversity, partitioned beta diversity into turnover and nestedness components, and evaluated how saline–alkaline conditions are associated with assemblage and diversity. Our results showed salinization in wetlands was often associated with high pH, nutrient enrichment, shallower surface water and lower macrophyte coverage, association with a significant decline in local phytoplankton diversity but no significant effect on rotifer diversity. Rotifer assemblages were mainly shaped by water depth, and macrophyte coverage, while phytoplankton assemblages were more influenced by TOC, NH4+-N, water temperature, and macrophyte coverage. Phytoplankton diversity in local wetlands was negatively associated with pH and inorganic nitrogen concentrations, whereas rotifer diversity was associated with water temperature, water depth, and nutrient concentrations. Despite these contrasting local responses, both groups exhibited high spatial compositional dissimilarity among investigated wetlands. Mean total beta diversity reached 0.89 for rotifers and 0.91 for phytoplankton, with turnover accounting for 74.16% and 67.03% of the assemblage dissimilarities, respectively. These findings reveal the profound impacts of freshwater salinization and alkalization on wetland organisms. We highlight the importance of integrating both alpha and beta diversity dimensions in monitoring biodiversity response to these emerging threats in freshwater ecosystems under global environmental change.
ndebd58fb7444: IntroductionHabitat degradation and conservation gaps severely threaten China's endemic montane birds, yet few studies have integrated habitat suitability with quality assessment.MethodsUsing the nationally protected Giant Laughingthrush (Garrulax maximus) across five provinces in western China and the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, we coupled optimized MaxEnt, InVEST, and GIS approaches to quantify potential distribution, habitat quality, conservation gaps, and environmental drivers. ResultsThe MaxEnt model performed robustly (mean AUC = 0.946). Climate dominated distribution (69.3% cumulative contribution), with annual precipitation (bio12, 35.7%) as the core limiting factor. The species occupied a cold-humid niche: annual precipitation 631.60–794.65 mm, driest-quarter temperature −7.12–2.75 °C, and elevation 2496.79–4012.78 m. High-suitability areas centered on the western Sichuan Basin rim, decreasing outward. Notably, a spatial mismatch emerged between habitat quality and suitability: Yunnan held the largest high-quality habitat (17.28 × 104 km2) but limited priority conservation areas, whereas Sichuan, with less high-quality habitat (13.63 × 104 km2), contained the largest priority zones (6.95 × 104 km2), indicating complementarity rather than substitution. Conservation gaps were extensive (54.26%–75.98%), mainly along reserve boundaries and buffers, revealing structural deficiencies from overemphasizing core zones while neglecting corridors. DiscussionThese findings underscore the urgency of reassessing and expanding protected area networks to cover priority zones. Our integrated framework offers a scientific reference for conserving the Giant Laughingthrush and managing montane birds within the Hengduan Mountains biodiversity hotspot, with implications for broader conservation planning in ecologically sensitive regions.
n61d8cbc1d728: We examined whether leaf water status, stomatal traits, and biochemical markers followed a common site ranking or formed contrasting response profiles in three public-space stands of Echinacea purpurea ‘Prairie Splendor’ in Budapest, Hungary. The stands occupied a roadside bed at the edge of Vérmező Park, the paved transport hub at Baross Square, and a bed within Pope John Paul II Square park. Microclimate was recorded on 24–26 July 2025, and leaves were sampled on 26 July. Vapour pressure deficit (VPD) and relative water content (RWC) were interpreted alongside stomatal traits, antioxidant-enzyme activities, proline, pigments, and extractable protein. One composite soil sample per site characterised soil chemistry, enzyme activities, and microbiological profiles. At Baross Square, lower mean VPD (1.89 kPa) accompanied a mean RWC of 98.36%. Mean RWC was 97.29% at Attila Street under greater atmospheric drying demand and 84.64% at Pope John Paul II Square, although the latter two sites had nearly identical maximum VPD. The Attila Street profile included shorter, denser stomata, the highest class III peroxidase (POD) and catalase (CAT) activities, and the highest mean proline content. Pope John Paul II Square had the highest mean pigment and extractable-protein contents on a fresh-weight basis. Total superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity and the air pollution tolerance index (APTI) showed no significant site differences, while individual APTI components varied. The descriptive soil profiles distinguished Attila Street, where higher relative organic-matter and phosphorus fractions, microbial respiration, fungal abundance, and functional microbial groups accompanied high RWC. Leaf water status, stomatal traits, and biochemical markers did not share a common site ranking. Their contrasting combinations indicate that leaf hydration alone only partly characterises the physiological state of these urban stands.

nb8d9fab57611: Marine heat waves (MHW) are important stressors on coral reefs, and evaluating their implications for the population dynamics of young corals has become a key research need. However, projecting the effects of MHW on the demographics of young corals is made difficult by an incomplete understanding of how their response to high temperature is modulated by light. Here we tested for the interactive effects of temperature and light on genetically identified colonies of the Pacific coral, Pocillopora spp. from 3-m depth in the back reef of Moorea, French Polynesia. The ecological implications of the responses to manipulated temperature and light were strengthened through context provided by long-term in situ records of temperature and light. Two 14-day trials were conducted in which young P. meandrina were exposed to 28°C and 31°C at six light levels ranging from 436 to 1621 μmol photons m−2 s−1. The probability of bleaching was unaffected by temperature, but it increased across the light gradient, while the probability of partial or full mortality increased with light faster at 31°C compared to 28°C. Mortality was associated with a decline in the photophysiological performance (F v/F m) of the symbiotic algae (Symbiodiniaceae) in the corals, notably as light levels increased at 31°C but not at 28°C, and at light levels commonly reached at 3-m depth. Declines in F v/F m revealed impaired PSII functionality, although values remained higher than those usually associated with bleaching (i.e., < 0.500). These results show how light can modulate the impacts of MHWs on the physiology and demography (i.e., survival) of young Pocillopora spp., and show that corals pale enough to be scored as fully bleached on the reef can contain relict algal populations that remain photophysiologically functional at elevated temperature and high light.
n2ebe3fafa633: Artificial reefs are widely used to enhance fishery resources and restore degraded marine habitats, yet quantitative information on the spatial responses of biological communities to reef distance remains limited in tropical marine ranching systems. This study investigated the spatial response distances of different catch groups to reef distance in the Wuzhizhou Island marine ranch, Sanya, Hainan Province, China. Based on five surveys conducted at 28 stations from 2019 to 2021, a total of 263 species of catches were collected using five sampling methods angling, gill net, trap, diving sampling, and bottom trawling. The catches were classified into five groups total catches, reef-dependent, reef-approaching, sand-mud bottom-preference, and strong-swimming. Generalized additive models (GAMs) were fitted using the Shannon-Wiener diversity (H), Pielou evenness (J), Margalef richness (d), and the Index of Relative Importance (IRI) as response variables. GAMs were used to characterize the relationships between community indices and reef distance, with additional sampling-method-adjusted models conducted to evaluate sensitivity to sampling heterogeneity. The strong-swimming group the reef-distance smooths were nonsignificant for all indices examined; no transition response distance was reported. The estimated response distances spanned 830–1120 m for the total catches group, 1420–1560 m for the reef-approaching group, and 1100–1450 m for the sand-mud bottom-preference group, whereas a single transition response distance of 890 m was identified for the reef-dependent group. These results demonstrate group-specific spatial responses to reef distance and provide quantitative reference information for spatial assessment and differentiated management of tropical marine ranching systems.
n8631a5c943cb: Rhythmic lunar and solar cycles are well recognised to influence the biology, behaviour, physiology, and ecological adaptations of many terrestrial organisms, yet their effects on marine organisms remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the influence of lunar and solar rhythms, together with total cloud cover as a light-blocking factor, on the acoustic behaviour of nine vocally active cetacean species, one pinniped species, and one fish species off Antarctica, the sub-Antarctic region, and the west coast of South Africa. These marine organisms exhibited species-, season-, and site-specific behavioural responses to cloud cover, lunar and solar rhythms. Total cloud cover, lunar phase or solar altitude (or, on a few occasions, moonlight intensity/lunar altitude) were the most important predictors of the observed acoustic behaviour. Observed behavioural changes related to light availability were also associated with breeding and migration phenology, communication, foraging and predator-avoidance strategies of the studied animals. On the whole, light availability drives the acoustic ecology and chronobiology of marine mammals and fish, likely as adaptations to their dynamic marine environments. Shifts in acoustic and diving behaviour relative to light availability have conservation implications, as sound production may reflect time spent near the sea surface and increase animals’ vertical risk of ship-strike. These predictable chronobiological patterns provide an empirical foundation for dynamic marine spatial management, suggesting that seasonal vessel slowdowns during dark-sky cycles could significantly reduce anthropogenic ship-strike risk in high-traffic zones like the South African coast.
n5cfa891be9a1: Camera trap surveys have become central to terrestrial wildlife monitoring, yet the route from raw detections to defensible inference is long, and in R it is walked with many single‐purpose packages. Researchers therefore spend disproportionate effort reshaping data and writing glue pipelines to move it between tools, and that effort peaks in density estimation for unmarked populations, where current guidance to compare several estimators is what the tooling makes hardest. In addition, there are few tools for behavioural and interspecific analyses of camera trap data. We present ct, an R package that carries an entire camera trap study from raw image metadata through cleaning, temporal‐independence filtering, effort accounting, modelling, and visualisation within a single tidy data structure. The package wraps and harmonises existing engines behind one consistent interface and extends the ecosystem with analyses it has lacked. At its core, ct places six density and abundance estimators for unmarked populations (camera trap distance sampling, random encounter model, time‐to‐event, space‐to‐event, instantaneous sampling, and the random encounter and staying‐time model) behind one interface, and documents for each the implementation it builds on, the data it requires, and the basis of its uncertainty interval. It also adds three analyses that, to our knowledge, no other camera trap package provides: an encounter response model that detects directed short‐term changes in one species' detection rate after another passes; a temporal shift statistic that measures how the diel activity window of a species moves between periods; and a spatial coverage surface that summarises where a species was detected. We demonstrate each capability on camera trap surveys from Benin and Taï National Park, Côte d'Ivoire. By standardising the workflow end to end, placing six density estimators behind one interface, adding new methods and providing data exploration utilities, ct lowers the technical cost of multi‐method camera trap ecology and brings reproducible analyses within reach of a much wider range of users. Résumé Les pièges photographiques sont devenus centraux dans le suivi de la faune terrestre, mais le chemin qui mène des détections brutes à une inférence solide est long et, dans R, il s'effectue à l'aide de nombreux packages à usage unique. Les chercheurs consacrent ainsi un effort disproportionné à remettre les données en forme et à écrire des scripts de liaison pour les faire circuler d'un outil à l'autre. C'est dans l'estimation de la densité des populations non marquées que cet effort est le plus lourd. Or, la recommandation actuelle d'y comparer plusieurs estimateurs est précisément ce que les outils rendent le plus difficile. En outre, peu d'outils existent pour les analyses comportementales et interspécifiques des données de pièges photographiques. Nous présentons ct, un package R qui accompagne l'intégralité d'une étude par pièges photographiques, des métadonnées brutes des images jusqu'à la modélisation et à la visualisation, en passant par le nettoyage, le filtrage pour l'indépendance temporelle et le calcul de l'effort. Toutes ces étapes s'effectuent au sein d'une même structure de données « tidy ». Le package encapsule et harmonise des moteurs existants derrière une interface cohérente, et enrichit l'écosystème d'analyses qui lui faisaient jusqu'ici défaut. Au cœur de ct, six estimateurs de densité et d'abondance pour les populations non marquées (échantillonnage par distances avec pièges photographiques, modèle de rencontre aléatoire, temps‐avant‐événement, espace‐avant‐événement, échantillonnage instantané et modèle de rencontre aléatoire et de temps de séjour) sont réunis derrière une interface unique. Pour chacun, ct documente l'implémentation sur laquelle il s'appuie, les données qu'il requiert et le fondement de son intervalle d'incertitude.…
n984090b50bca: Time‐calibrated species tree of Petrocodon. Summary Whether evolutionary radiations are primarily driven by ecological or neutral processes remains an unresolved question. The karst‐endemic genus Petrocodon, distributed across southern China and northern Indochina, provides a powerful system for testing these alternatives. We generated whole‐genome sequencing data for 54 of the 60 described species and integrated these with morphological, geographic, and paleoclimatic data to evaluate the relative roles of ecological and neutral processes in diversification. Our analyses revealed a robust nuclear phylogeny but extensive cytonuclear discordance, likely due to pervasive ancient hybridization and introgression. Macroevolutionary and biogeographic analyses indicate that diversification began during a favorable climatic period enabling range expansion, but subsequent species accumulation was primarily driven by geographic isolation and allopatric divergence rather than ecological niche differentiation. Morphological evolution decoupled from lineage diversification, with most morphological diversity accumulating relatively late. Further analyses support genetic drift in small, isolated populations driving morphological evolution, although stabilizing selection cannot be excluded, and reticulate evolution may have additionally contributed to phenotypic innovation. Together, these results support a largely nonadaptive radiation in Petrocodon, in which spatial opportunity played a central role in species accumulation, while demographic and reticulate processes may have contributed to its striking phenotypic diversity.
n300c938af9ff: Conceptual diagram of rhizosphere metabolite‐mediated recruitment of P‐solubilizing bacteria for enhanced P acquisition. Summary Low phosphorus (P) availability limits citrus production, while genotypic determinants governing rhizosphere P mobilization remain elusive. Here, we investigated P‐acquisition strategies in citrus rootstocks. We performed a systematic screening of citrus rootstocks under P‐deficient conditions and identified two contrasting genotypes: P‐efficient Citrus tangerina and P‐inefficient Citrus junos. Comparative metabolomics, microbiome profiling, targeted strain isolation, and inoculation assays were combined to unravel metabolic and microbial drivers governing P mobilization. The superior P acquisition of C. tangerina stemmed from a unique root‐exudate profile enriched in 2‐hydroxyflavanone, scopoletin, raffinose, and gallic acid. These metabolites selectively enriched Methylobacterium sp. strain HA110, a robust P‐solubilizing bacterium. Exogenous exudate application enhanced C. junos P acquisition, yet this beneficial effect was abolished under soil sterilization, demonstrating an essential role of microbiota. Combined supplementation of the metabolites and strain HA110 enhanced rhizosphere P activation, which in turn strengthened the P‐acquisition capacity of C. junos and consequently stimulated its growth. Collectively, these findings uncover a novel metabolite–microbe axis: P‐efficient rootstocks reshape their rhizosphere microbiome through specific exudates. This axis is amenable to rational reconfiguration to restore P acquisition in P‐inefficient genotypes, laying a theoretical basis for exudate‐derived biofertilizers to boost P‐use efficiency in sustainable citriculture.
nee43b3302113: Environmental changes are predominant drivers of species range dynamics, bringing new species into contact and forming novel biotic interactions. Yet we know little about how novel interactions affect range changes. We propose that biotic permeability—the degree to which species assemblages are permeable to individuals of a range-shifting species—may help anticipate range changes. Biotic permeability balances biotic resistance from negative interactions and biotic potential from positive interactions. We present a trait-based approach to estimate biotic permeability and to infer a theoretical biotic range limit where resistance and potential are balanced. Mapping biotic permeability reveals areas where future range expansions, contractions, and shifts are likely, enabling predictions about the direction and intensity of range changes.
n8340af69e2a7: Artificial propagation, wildlife farming, ranching, cultivation, and aquaculture support commercial markets and livelihoods, and their products may be promoted as substitutes for wild harvest. However, production labels for these products cannot be used to determine conservation benefit because output may depend on wild inputs. Thus, we developed hidden wild‐input (HWI) accounting as a bounded assessment framework. HWIs are wild‐derived biological inputs that are important for producing substitutes but also potentially for conservation, and they are underrepresented in labels, statistics, and assessments. Through conceptual analysis and comparison, we identified establishment, maintenance, and scaling production inputs and conducted a counterfactual evaluation to determine the avoided harvest of wild targets, source‐population burdens, and other ecological effects, such as wild‐input intensity, wild‐origin proportion, supplementation frequency, and elasticity. We examined four examples of wild‐input use to illustrate the framework: Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) source code Y exposed the gap between production‐origin categories and upstream accounting; crocodile ranching showed recurring wild inputs can coexist with conservation gains under regulated management; capture‐based European eel (Anguilla anguilla) aquaculture demonstrated production–extraction coupling; and the artificial production of Chinese caterpillar fungus (Ophiocordyceps sinensis) revealed potential commercial dependence when recurring inputs are not reported. Together, the examples showed that source categories cannot be used to quantify upstream burdens, recurring inputs do not indicate conservation failure, and input–output coefficients demonstrate coupling but not net effects. Conservation benefit should be assessed against a credible no‐expansion counterfactual by asking whether additional output reduces target harvest, added wild‐input burdens remain sustainable, and other ecological effects reverse the gain. Complete biological independence is neither necessary nor sufficient. When input, demographic, and market‐substitution data are unavailable, uncertainty should be reported rather than replaced by assumptions based on production labels. Atención a los insumos silvestres ocultos en los sustitutos para la conservación Resumen La reproducción artificial, la cría de fauna silvestre, la ganadería, el cultivo y la acuicultura sustentan los mercados comerciales y los medios de vida, y sus productos pueden promocionarse como sustitutos de la recolección silvestre. Sin embargo, las etiquetas de producción de estos productos no pueden utilizarse para determinar el beneficio para la conservación, ya que la producción puede depender de insumos silvestres. Por ello, hemos desarrollado la contabilidad de los insumos silvestres ocultos (HWI) como un marco de evaluación delimitado. Los HWI son insumos biológicos de origen silvestre que resultan importantes para la producción de sustitutos, pero también, potencialmente, para la conservación, y que están infrarrepresentados en las etiquetas, las estadísticas y las evaluaciones. nafcb223adcd2: To halt and reverse rapid biodiversity loss, countries are pursuing the ambitious goals and targets in the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) to restore and protect biodiversity in representative networks of protected areas. However, the associated monitoring framework lacks indicators of ecosystem representativeness for Target 3. Using South Africa as an example, we tested different indicators that could fill this gap and made recommendations for globally relevant options for national and international reporting. Specifically, we calculated seven indicators that use different combinations of data on protected areas, ecosystem types, and ecological condition. We used these indicators to measure progress in effective, representative ecosystem protection at different scales in South Africa: country, ecosystem group (e.g., realm), and ecosystem type. The indicators revealed more informative insights, such as which ecosystem types are best progressing toward meeting their protection targets and where protection levels could improve if degraded habitat within protected areas was restored, than protected area coverage (PAC; total % protection). We tabulated the data requirements, advantages, and disadvantages for the indicators and provided recommendations for their use. We recommend condition‐adjusted representativeness (CAR) and the ecosystem protection level index be added as component indicators in the GBF monitoring framework for Target 3. These two indicators could also be assessed using the Global Ecosystem Typology (GET) for standardized aggregation or disaggregation of ecosystem types at different levels. For single time points, plotting PAC, representativeness, CAR, and ecosystem protection level by ecosystem functional groups (GET level 3) can be informative. Applying these indicators can strengthen biodiversity reporting under the GBF. Indicadores para rastrear los avances de la protección efectiva de los ecosistemas representativos Resumen Para detener y revertir la rápida pérdida de biodiversidad, los países están persiguiendo los ambiciosos objetivos y metas del Marco Global de Biodiversidad (GBF) de Kunming‐Montreal con el fin de restaurar y proteger la biodiversidad en redes representativas de áreas protegidas. Sin embargo, el marco de seguimiento asociado carece de indicadores de representatividad de los ecosistemas para la Meta 3. Con Sudáfrica como ejemplo, evaluamos diferentes indicadores que podrían subsanar esta carencia y formulamos recomendaciones sobre opciones de relevancia mundial para la presentación de informes a nivel nacional e internacional. En concreto, calculamos siete indicadores que utilizan diferentes combinaciones de datos sobre áreas protegidas, tipos de ecosistemas y estado ecológico. Utilizamos estos indicadores para medir los avances en la protección eficaz y representativa de los ecosistemas a diferentes escalas en Sudáfrica: a nivel nacional, de grupo de ecosistemas (p. ej., reino) y de tipo de ecosistema. Los indicadores revelaron información más relevante, como qué tipos de ecosistemas están avanzando mejor hacia el cumplimiento de sus objetivos de protección y en qué casos podrían mejorarse los niveles de protección si se restauraran los hábitats degradados dentro de las áreas protegidas, que la cobertura de las áreas protegidas (PAC; porcentaje total de protección). Estos dos indicadores también podrían evaluarse utilizando la Tipología Global de Ecosistemas (GET) para la agregación o desagregación estandarizada de los tipos de ecosistemas a diferentes niveles.…
nc5475f95f946: Functional diversity (FD) is widely used to study ecosystem processes, leading to the continuous development of FD metrics. However, the proliferation of these descriptors raises concerns regarding structural redundancy, particularly in ecological modelling, where the simultaneous use of highly concordant FD metrics may compromise model parsimony. We propose a multi‐stage approach to diagnose structural redundancy among selected FD metrics when theoretical, mathematical, or empirical considerations suggest overlap, using complementary analyses across continuous and categorised representations. We illustrate the approach through two pairwise comparisons: the community‐based weighted functional dendrogram index (wFDc), which incorporates the species community pool, versus richness–quadratic entropy (RQ) and Rao's quadratic entropy (Q) versus functional dispersion (FDis). The framework was applied to both metric pairs using benthic macroinvertebrate assemblages from three contrasting freshwater ecosystems in Ecuador. Both metric pairs exhibited high concordance across the three ecosystems, with strong continuous associations and substantial agreement in percentile‐based classifications. By incorporating richness‐controlled analyses, the framework evaluates whether concordance persists after accounting for shared richness dependence. For both pairs, residual associations remained strong, supporting suspected structural overlap in the examined datasets. Our findings suggest that the simultaneous use of highly concordant FD metrics could be unnecessary. Rather than questioning the development of new FD metrics, the proposed framework provides a practical diagnostic protocol for evaluating their structural redundancy. To facilitate its application, we provide the R package FD Concordance https://github.com/Gonpa83/FD_concordance.git and a companion Shiny application of the same name https://01a168d6‐1a69‐a0e6‐7a29‐7e329e9dbbdb.share.connect.posit.cloud/ enabling researchers to apply the protocol to their own index values. These tools support targeted assessments of suspected overlap and more parsimonious ecological modelling and biomonitoring.
nec86f36b16bf: Rapid and accurate assessment of insect communities is increasingly important in the context of climate change and biodiversity loss. Environmental DNA (eDNA) analysis has proven useful as a noninvasive method for detecting insects in aquatic systems, and methods for terrestrial eDNA sources are being developed. Analysis of wildflower‐associated DNA may be useful for identifying insect pollinators. This study paired traditional butterfly netting surveys in a montane protected area with wildflower‐associated eDNA metabarcoding to test whether the presence and abundance of butterfly species can be accurately assessed. Specifically, Lepidoptera targeting primers were used to amplify two regions of the cytochrome oxidase subunit I (COI) gene from wildflower‐associated eDNA samples. Analysis of the ~350 million sequences obtained identified ~94% as insects, with ~23% assigned to Lepidoptera. Six butterfly taxa, including four at the species level, were identified, including five that were consistent with species captured during netting surveys conducted in parallel. However, butterfly detections from eDNA did not correspond with either contrived or natural flower visitation, and traditional surveys identified 44 butterfly species not captured by eDNA. The most prevalently detected taxa were small‐bodied insects closely associated with flowers. Together our results indicate that additional refinement of protocols and primers is needed before wildflower‐associated eDNA can reliably survey butterfly species.
n7f291b951cd2: Individual bird tracking can resolve continuous migration processes but is limited by small sample sizes, whereas citizen‐science records provide broad spatial and multi‐year coverage but are affected by observation effort and spatial accessibility. However, few studies have evaluated how citizen‐science records and individual tracking correspond across both spatial and temporal components of the same migratory system, including migration routes, stopover sites, migration timing, and broad‐scale spatial coverage. We integrated 105,630 valid satellite locations from 22 rescued and released Eastern Buzzards (Buteo japonicus), of which 10 completed 27 full migrations, with 25,651 records of this species from eBird and GBIF. We compared the two data sources in terms of migration routes and continental‐scale latitudinal coverage, repeatedly used stopover sites, migration timing, and landscape composition. Both data sources revealed northward migration in spring and southward migration in autumn. The latitudinal spans represented by citizen‐science records were 661 km narrower in spring and 937 km narrower in autumn than those derived from tracking. Five of the 10 repeatedly used stopover sites identified by satellite tracking had citizen‐science records within 100 km during the corresponding migration season. The overlap coefficients between their 24‐h distributions were 0.594 in spring and 0.585 in autumn. Bray–Curtis similarity in landscape composition between the two data sources was 0.545. These results show that the two data sources provide convergent evidence of seasonal migration progression and continental‐scale movements, while local differences highlight potential gaps in citizen‐science coverage.
n98c7e1907d00: The sustainable management of small-scale fisheries is key for the well-being of coastal communities. Environmental conditions are known to influence the ecology of the coastal zone, yet their interactions with fisheries management regimes remains poorly understood. We examined spatial changes in the structure of benthic communities under distinct management regimes (TURF or Territorial Use Rights for Fisheries, and OA or open access areas) located in areas with different temperature patterns (warm and cold). Using underwater visual censuses, we assessed benthic community patterns across four locations in northern-central Chile and examined how species diversity and composition varied between management and environmental regimes. Our results showed that communities differed significantly between management and temperature regimes. In general, sessile community richness was 65% higher under cold regimes compared to warm regimes. For mobile invertebrates, richness and diversity were 42% and 41% greater in TURF areas than in OA areas, while both attributes were 4% and 5% higher under cold than warm temperature regimes. In the case of fish communities, species composition varied as a function of the interaction between management and temperature regimes. In cold sites, benthic communities within TURF areas were characterized by the kelp Lessonia trabeculata, the whelk Concholepas concholepas, and keyhole limpets (Fissurella spp.), whereas OA areas were dominated by kelp, the sea urchin Arbacia nigra, and the starfish Meyenaster gelatinosus. Benthic communities of TURF areas in warm sites were associated with anemones, sea urchins and kelps, whereas OA areas were dominated mainly by anemones and sea urchins. Overall, our results support the notion that the structure of benthic communities can be influenced by an interaction between management regime and environmental conditions. The two temperature regimes stem from the differential exposure to coastal upwelling between sites, which suggests that other environmental processes, such as productivity or wave exposure, are implicated. Overall, the marked ecological differences between TURF and OA areas under contrasting temperature patterns suggest that environmental conditions should be incorporated into the design of novel fishery policies to promote the sustainable management of small-scale coastal fisheries.
n64ef4599d7f3: Mesozoic lungfishes are often represented in the fossil record by isolated tooth plates, which impose limitations on their taxonomic identification and on the interpretation of their diversity. In the Triassic of South America, these organisms remain poorly documented. The present study describes eight isolated tooth plates from the Candelária Sequence of the Santa Maria Supersequence (Carnian, Late Triassic), southern Brazil, being attributed to three taxa: Ptychoceratodus phillipsi, P. eliseui sp. nov., and Ferganoceratodus cabreirai sp. nov. The description was made using morphological and morphometric approaches and the tooth plates. The results highlight the strong morphological similarity between Ptychoceratodus and Ferganoceratodus, as well as the overlap of diagnostic characters, which reinforces the difficulties in distinguishing between these genera when only isolated tooth plates are available. The association with other ichthyofauna and the presence of deposits indicative of varying depositional energies suggest a seasonal environment, with alternation between wet and dry periods. From a paleobiogeographic perspective, the record of Ferganoceratodus represents the first occurrence of the genus in the Triassic of South America, extending its previously known distribution. The occurrence of P. phillipsi, in turn, reinforces the wide dispersal of lungfishes throughout Pangaea during the Mesozoic. In this context, the materials described herein represent a relevant contribution to the Gondwanan record of Mesozoic lungfishes and reinforce the importance of the Candelária Sequence as a key unit for Triassic dipnoan paleobiogeography and biostratigraphy. The occurrence of these genera in Brazilian continental deposits is consistent with the distribution pattern observed for Mesozoic lungfishes and suggests faunal affinities with assemblages from other portions of Gondwana.
n08572b9aa114: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Acquiring a critical understanding of how organisms respond to environmental changes requires integrating molecular and whole‐organism perspectives while investigating how latitudinal gradients shape thermal responses. We explored trade‐offs between thermal tolerance and performance in the marine intertidal gastropod Littorina littorea collected from 10 locations across a wide latitudinal gradient in North America. Snails were exposed under laboratory conditions to a wide range of temperatures (from 5 to 27°C) for 30 days, after which we characterised their metabolomic profiles in relation to whole‐organism responses obtained from a previous study on the same individuals, including growth, feeding rate, metabolic rate and critical thermal maximum (CTmax). Relationships between growth, feeding rate, CTmax and one major metabolomic axis revealed clear trade‐offs between fitness‐related traits and thermal tolerance. The decreased concentrations of metabolites contributing most to such trade‐offs were negatively associated with growth and feeding but positively associated with CTmax. Many of these metabolites also differed consistently among locations, with individuals from warmer (lower latitude) regions showing lower concentrations. Their higher concentrations in snails from colder environments may provide them with a greater metabolic capacity, potentially relaxing the trade‐off between thermal tolerance and fitness. Highly abundant metabolites in snails from colder locations were often linked to antioxidant and cellular stress responses. Furthermore, metabolites linearly and non‐linearly related to temperature showed variation in their thermal sensitivity depending on the location, with snails from colder sites showing greater thermal responses. Our results suggest that increased thermal tolerance may come at the expense of reduced investments in fitness‐related traits. The relaxed trade‐offs, the higher production of cellular heat stress defences and the enhanced metabolomic thermal response of snails from colder regions may explain their higher thermal tolerance and acclimation capacity. We show how energy metabolism trade‐offs can shape species thermal tolerance variation across broad environmental gradients. The integrated whole‐organism and molecular perspective we provide offers new insights into the potential adaptive mechanisms governing species responses to current and future climate change. n695a3e78f7fa: Land‐use changes induced by human activities usually accelerate soil erosion, leading to losses of soil organic matter (SOM). The mechanisms by which cultivation‐associated degradation affects SOM composition via changes of content and quality of particulate (POM), mineral‐associated (MAOM), dissolved organic matter (DOM), and microbial biomass are not elucidated. We investigated the C:N stoichiometry of these fractions, and erosion (using 137Cs activity) along a chronosequence of cultivation‐associated degradation (0–114 years) in Mollisols. Two‐pool and Bayesian three‐source mixing models estimated contributions of microbial biomass, DOM, and POM to MAOM to the total SOM. Erosion intensity ranged locally from 440 to 4800 t km−2 year−1, resulting in cumulative soil losses of 11,000 to 320,000 t km−2 over 114 years of cultivation. As cultivation duration and eroded amounts increased, the C/N ratios of POM, MAOM, and DOM declined owing to (i) the faster loss of C than N, (ii) a decrease in C/N with soil depth involved in tillage horizon, and (iii) N input by fertilization. These higher C than N losses reflect that erosion is not the sole process leading to the decline of C stocks, but intensive cultivation also accelerates organic matter mineralization and CO2 release to the atmosphere. As the C/N ratios of POM and MAOM declined but microbial C/N increased, the estimated contribution of microbial inputs to MAOM increased from 6% to 32%. The Bayesian model partitioned MAOM sources into DOM (8%), microbial (11%), and POM (81%), reinforcing that POM dominates MAOM formation in croplands. Cultivation‐associated degradation led to SOC losses by reducing POM‐C/N and MAOM‐C/N ratios, while erosion strongly accelerated these effects. Furthermore, cultivation‐associated degradation is also based on the limited inputs of organic C as the precursors for MAOM formation by depleting POM. These results from a > 100‐year chronosequence indicate that cultivation‐induced degradation reduces SOM content, while also shifting the MAOM composition progressively towards a greater contribution of microbial C.
nb98da579c1b6: Permafrost regions store vast quantities of soil organic carbon (SOC), yet the future trajectories of functionally distinct SOC fractions across soil depths remain poorly constrained. Integrating depth‐explicit soil fractionation data from 104 sites across the Tibetan permafrost region with a process‐based SOC model, we project century‐scale dynamics of particulate (POC) and mineral‐associated organic carbon (MAOC) under three emission scenarios. We show that MAOC currently comprises 56.5% of regional total SOC stock and remains far from saturation throughout the profile. Consistent with this large stabilization capacity, total SOC was projected to increase over the 21st century under all scenarios, with the largest gains under SSP5‐8.5. However, this positive net gain masked a significant restructuring of SOC fractions. MAOC accumulated across all depths and scenarios, and heavy POC remained comparatively buffered, whereas light POC declined under SSP5‐8.5. The strongest relative light POC losses occurred in the 10–30 cm layers, where warming‐driven decomposition remained strong while plant‐C input compensation weakened. These divergent trajectories indicate a shift toward a “carbon‐rich yet energy‐poor” state, where mineral‐bound carbon increases while the labile particulate pool supporting microbial activity is depleted. Our findings reveal SOC vulnerability in permafrost region is governed by both fraction identity and soil depth, and that net SOC gains can conceal the loss of metabolically active carbon. Incorporating measurable, depth‐resolved SOC fractions into Earth system models is therefore essential for constraining permafrost–climate feedbacks.
n79cabb410281: Nitrogen (N) input is expected to intensify phosphorus (P) limitation in tropical and subtropical forests. However, how soil and microbial processes mobilize P from poorly available pools to sustain soil P bioavailability remains unclear. We conducted a nine‐year experiment with low (20 kg N ha−1 year−1) and high (80 kg N ha−1 year−1) N addition treatments in a subtropical Moso bamboo (Phyllostachys edulis) plantation. We quantified soil P fractions, P‐cycling functional genes, phosphatase activity, P sorption capacity (PSC), iron and aluminum oxides, and plant properties throughout the experiment. Our results reveal three distinct stages in the regulation of soil bioavailable P with prolonged N addition. Phase I: N addition reduces P bioavailability, and labile organic P decomposition becomes the main source of bioavailable P, associated with increased phosphatase activity. Phase II: when labile organic P becomes insufficient to meet P demand, bioavailable P is replenished through the depletion of moderately labile organic P; this is related to decreased PSC and enhanced acid phosphomonoesterases activity. Phase III: stable organic P decreases significantly, jointly sustaining bioavailable P with the depletion of other organic P fractions, alongside a further decrease in PSC and enriched microbial organic acid‐ and phosphatase‐related genes. This study uncovers a novel “three‐phased P supply” model revealed through long‐term observations. These mechanistic insights reveal the pathways of soil P mobilization under continuous N input in a subtropical forest and establish a framework for predicting the buffering capacity of soil P pools in P‐limited ecosystems under global change scenarios.
nfc044222567c: Where does the future of a population reside? Reproductive value provides an answer. We show how new technologies could make this century‐old concept dynamic and individualised, and propose extending it to communities to reveal demographic resilience, portfolio effects and vulnerabilities that conventional measures of abundance may miss. Abstract Research Highlights: Lebreton, J.‐D., & Oli, M. K. (2026). Reproductive value as a key concept in ecology and evolutionary biology. Journal of Animal Ecology. https://doi.org/10.1111/1365‐2656.70343. Ecologists are good at counting things. Yet individuals are not interchangeable in what they contribute to a population's future. Lebreton and Oli's synthesis of reproductive value (RV) shows that this deceptively simple idea connects demographic theory, life‐history evolution, spatial ecology, epidemiology and conservation. Indeed, RV provides a common currency for asking not simply how many individuals occupy a population, but where its demographic future resides. Here, I highlight this unifying perspective and argue that new technologies could take RV from a predominantly class‐based quantity towards a dynamic, individualised and spatially explicit description of populations. Combining demographic models with biologging, automated monitoring, genomic information and ecological digital twins could reveal reproductive value at resolutions Fisher himself could scarcely have imagined. I further suggest that RV could enrich community‐stability theory by weighting species' fluctuations by their contribution to future population persistence, thereby connecting population resilience, biodiversity insurance and ecosystem stability.
nabf3221aa570: Humans have introduced non‐native species around the world. Once introduced species can become naturalised (self‐sustaining population) and invasive (spread with negative consequences). We characterised introduction biases, and quantified introduction debt in trees introduced to Australia. Australia's introduced trees were selectively introduced. They are therefore not a random subset of non‐native trees. Introductions have altered characteristics of Australia's tree flora. Abstract Humans have transported and introduced thousands of non‐native species around the world, some of which then naturalise and become invasive. Introduction bias indicates characteristics of non‐native species that have been preferentially introduced, which could subsequently bias characteristics associated with species invasiveness. Introduction debt captures non‐native species that have not yet been introduced but could be in the future, highlighting potential threats. We test for introduction bias and debt in non‐native trees introduced to Australia using a dataset of 57,958 tree species known globally. We examine trends in family, functional traits (height, seed mass, specific leaf area [SLA], wood density), home region, human uses and invasion history elsewhere. We test for biotic homogenisation by comparing the taxonomic and functional characteristics of trees introduced to Australia with Australia's 3114 native trees. Of 54,844 tree species that aren't native to Australia, 6066 have been introduced to Australia, of which 657 have become naturalised and 106 have become invasive. This leaves an introduction debt of 48,778 species. We found that species naturalised in numerous other countries and more heavily used by humans are more likely to have been introduced to Australia. Species from certain families (e.g. Arecaceae), countries (e.g. China) and continents (e.g. Europe) were more likely to have been introduced. Naturalised and invasive trees were more likely to originate from Europe. We detected introduction biases towards shorter and lighter‐seeded species, which were accentuated in the invasive species subset. Species with lower SLA have been preferentially introduced to Australia, but the mean SLA of non‐native trees was still higher than that of native trees. Differences between native and introduced trees across all four functional traits suggest that tree introductions have homogenised Australia's tree flora, making it more functionally similar to global tree flora. Synthesis. Australia's introduced trees are not a random subset of all non‐native trees but have been selectively introduced. Non‐native introductions have homogenised and altered characteristics of Australia's tree flora. Of the almost 49,000 tree species that could still be introduced, species from the tropics and South America pose an especially high future introduction risk for Australia.
n9dde299efd07: A working model of the ZmNAC41‐ZmABC‐ZmCP module in regulating SCR resistance. Summary Plant disease resistance is often governed by complex multigene modules, yet their composition and regulation remain poorly defined. Here, we identify a maize defense module comprising the NAC (NAM, ATAF1/2, and CUC2) transcription factor ZmNAC41, the PADRE domain‐containing protein ZmABC, and the cysteine protease ZmCP. This module contributes to resistance to southern corn rust (SCR) caused by Puccinia polysora and is linked to jasmonic acid (JA)‐associated defense responses. Upon pathogen infection, ZmNAC41 was rapidly induced and directly activated ZmABC transcription. ZmABC physically interacted with ZmCP. Increased JA accumulation and induction of JA biosynthetic and JA‐responsive genes were also observed. Silencing any one of the three genes markedly attenuated JA‐associated defense responses and compromised resistance, supporting a functional contribution of all three components to maize defense. Importantly, natural variation analysis identified elite haplotypes carrying favorable alleles of ZmNAC41, ZmABC, and ZmCP, and these allele combinations were significantly associated with enhanced field resistance. Together, our findings reveal a maize defense module that integrates transcriptional regulation and protein interaction and contributes to SCR resistance in association with JA‐associated defense responses. These findings provide genetic targets for breeding maize with improved resistance to SCR.
n4cf024ec776e: How does behavioral individuality arise? Theoretical models have highlighted the potential roles of genes and the environment. However, Gallagher et al. show that behavioral individuality occurs in the absence of genetic variation and is unaffected by experimentally manipulating the developmental environment. This suggests that behavioral individuality may originate even before birth.
na6a34cbcb8ea: Due to their rapid reproductive cycles and short generation times, small mammals—particularly rodents and shrews—are widely used as bioindicators in ecological studies. While traditional live trapping provides detailed demographic data for such monitoring, it is labour‐intensive and subject to sampling bias. In contrast, owl pellet analysis presents a non‐invasive and cost‐effective alternative for evaluating small mammal community structure over broad spatial and temporal scales, though potential prey preferences should be considered. This study evaluates the effectiveness of owl pellet analysis in comparison to conventional trapping methods for monitoring small mammal communities. We synthesised data from 26 published studies and additional unpublished field reports, comprising a uniquely robust dataset of 40 systematically processed case studies across seven countries in Central Europe, a biogeographically coherent region. In all cases, trapping and pellet collection were carried out at the same locations and during the same periods, allowing for an exceptional level of methodological consistency. Results reveal that owl pellet analysis detects higher species diversity and provides a more efficient, non‐invasive means of monitoring small mammal assemblages over larger spatial and temporal scales. However, prey preferences and hunting behaviour of owls introduce biases, often overrepresenting abundant prey such as the common vole, Microtus arvalis and underrepresenting species associated with specific habitats or microclimates. These biases have significant implications for biodiversity assessments and paleoenvironmental reconstructions, where accurate community composition is essential. Our findings indicate that while owl pellet analysis is a valuable tool for ecological monitoring, careful consideration of predator selectivity is necessary to accurately interpret the results. Further research into owl hunting ecology is recommended to refine the application of this method in biodiversity studies and paleoecology.
nbad7735a4b77: Peatlands provide critical ecosystem services, including carbon storage, water regulation, and climate mitigation, yet spatial information on their ecological condition remains limited despite widespread degradation. Specific biogeochemical analyses (e.g., biomarkers, molecular compounds, compound specific stable isotopes) can characterize drainage‐related changes in peat properties but are time‐consuming, costly, linked to sophisticated analytical set‐up and thus spatially restricted. We therefore investigated whether high‐resolution PlanetScope imagery capture consistent spectral differences between pristine and drained areas and explored their multivariate correspondence with complementary site‐level biogeochemical properties. Spectral indices, including NDVI, EVI, gNDVI, Greenness Index, and albedo were derived from PlanetScope Analysis‐Ready Surface Reflectance (ARPS) data for nine European peatland sites spanning three climatic zones and contrasting open and sparsely treed vegetation structures. Peat biogeochemistry was characterized using elemental carbon and nitrogen contents and molecular composition determined by pyrolysis–GC/MS. NDVI and Greenness Index differed most consistently between the investigated pristine and drained areas, with higher values under drained conditions across both vegetation structures. In contrast, EVI and albedo, even though also suitable indicators, depended more strongly on vegetation structure and the patterns differed between open and sparsely treed systems. Spectral differences were most pronounced during May and June, identifying the early growing season as the period of strongest spectral separation within the investigated dataset. Drained areas were additionally characterized by higher nitrogen contents, lower C/N ratios, and a greater relative abundance of compounds indicative of metabolized organic matter. Exploratory principal component analyses indicated complementary site‐level patterns between spectral and biogeochemical variables associated with hydrological condition. Consequently, this study demonstrates the potential of high‐resolution PlanetScope spectral data to differentiate between pristine and drained peatland conditions across the investigated sites. However, predictive classification of previously unknown peatland areas will require dedicated modeling and independent validation especially in differentiating from surrounding transition peats and mineral grassland soils.
naffe86a4943a: Song amplitude is an important but comparatively understudied dimension of avian acoustic communication, influencing signal transmission, detectability and social interactions. We investigated ecological and structural drivers of song amplitude variation in six passerine species using 3265 songs recorded from 120 territorial males. Body size was associated with cross‐species variation in amplitude only when the largest and loudest species, the Great Reed Warbler, was included. Across species, song amplitude declined with increasing temperature, relative humidity and time after sunrise, whereas ambient noise showed no evidence of a generalised Lombard effect. Song rate, song length and peak frequency were consistent predictors of amplitude, with peak frequency showing the strongest association. Within‐species analyses revealed substantial heterogeneity in environmental effects, whereas relationships between amplitude and song structure were more consistent across species. Individual identity explained considerable variation in amplitude, indicating pronounced within‐species variability in vocal output. Overall, our results suggest that song amplitude is a flexible component of vocal performance shaped primarily by song structure and signalling context rather than by body size alone. These findings emphasise the importance of considering both behavioural and ecological sources of variation when interpreting patterns of acoustic signalling in birds.
ndf347faee216: Based on genome‐wide SNP data, this study assessed genomic diversity and population structure in Tibetan antelopes sampled from the Selincuo National Nature Reserve. The analyses included runs of homozygosity (ROH), genomic inbreeding coefficients, genetic diversity, linkage disequilibrium (LD), effective population size, genomic relatedness, principal component analysis (PCA), and sNMF. Genomic inbreeding varied among the sampled individuals, with substantial variation among individuals. Short and medium‐length ROHs predominated, whereas long ROHs contributed little to total ROH coverage. This pattern indicates that population‐wide homozygosity is mainly associated with older shared ancestry, genetic drift, and historical demographic change, with limited evidence of severe recent inbreeding. Several individuals had relatively high ROH‐based inbreeding coefficients, indicating heterogeneous individual‐level autozygosity. The samples retained considerable genome‐wide SNP variation, although allele frequencies were unevenly distributed. PCA showed dispersion among individuals, while sNMF identified multiple ancestry components with substantial overlap in individual genetic backgrounds. Kinship analysis detected no first‐ or second‐degree relatives among the sampled individuals. Linkage disequilibrium declined with increasing physical distance between markers, providing a basis for estimating recent effective population size and evaluating demographic history. Overall, the analyzed individuals showed variation in genomic autozygosity, with several exhibiting elevated homozygosity. The LD‐based estimate of recent effective population size provides a baseline for continued genomic monitoring of Tibetan antelopes sampled from the Selincuo region. Broader geographic and temporal sampling is needed to assess population boundaries and changes in genetic diversity. Future work should expand sampling across geographic regions and time periods and compare multiple populations using genome‐wide differentiation, IBD sharing, isolation‐by‐distance analysis, demographic modeling, and direct estimates of migration or gene flow. These analyses will clarify historical demographic changes, recent effective population size variation, and genetic connectivity among protected areas.
n15c4b8e55ff4: The success of biological invasions depends strongly on the genetic diversity and dispersal abilities of invading populations. In many species, males and females differ in their dispersal behavior, potentially contributing unequally to the establishment and spread of invasive populations. Population genetic approaches provide powerful tools for investigating genetic diversity and dispersal patterns. When applied to populations in their native range, these approaches can improve our ability to predict the spread and potential impacts of species following their introduction into new environments. However, such studies remain scarce for many invasive species. This holds true for small hive beetles (SHB), Aethina tumida, which are free‐flying parasites of social bee colonies native to sub‐Saharan Africa that have recently become a widespread invasive species. Here, we show high gene flow across A. tumida populations from Western Kenya. Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and nuclear DNA (nuDNA) markers were used to study SHB genetic diversity and differentiation and to infer short‐ and medium‐range dispersal across host colonies (N = 15) and neighboring apiaries (N = 5; ≤ 30 km apart). The mtDNA diversity was high (29 haplotypes in 87 samples), but no significant differences were detected in haplotype diversity and distribution within and across apiaries. The nuDNA diversity and differentiation levels also did not differ significantly between apiaries. However, genetic differentiation among apiaries was significantly lower in males than in females. Moreover, significant isolation by distance was detected in the females but not in the males, suggesting sex‐biased dispersal. Overall, the results suggest that the observed high gene flow underlies the high genetic diversity of SHB, which may contribute to its invasion success.
n3a46d4852129: Woodpeckers are keystone species playing a crucial role as ecosystem engineers, with their highest species richness and diversity in the tropical and subtropical regions. Although most research on the species' ecology originates from the temperate regions, it leaves a substantial gap in woodpecker assemblage and nesting ecology in tropical and subtropical areas. Our study fills this gap in the subtropical region of South Asia, exploring woodpecker diversity, abundance, and factors influencing cavity nest occurrence in the lowland sal Shorea robusta forests of Nepal. The study was carried out in May and June 2024 in the Pathlaiya Community Forest (CF), with 24 line transects established. Each transect was surveyed twice for woodpecker abundance and nesting cavities, with data gathered on the perpendicular distance of woodpecker observation from the transect, tree characteristics, and nesting variables. Distance sampling analysis was used to estimate an overall woodpecker density and detection probability in the study area, which were found to be 0.54 ± 0.07 birds/ha and 0.79 ± 0.05, respectively. Overall, 51 individuals from nine woodpecker species were recorded. In Nepal's lowland sal forests, the nesting occurrence of woodpeckers was significantly influenced by factors: canopy cover, tree condition and tree Diameter at Breast Height (DBH), with emphasis on sal and jamun Syzygium cumini as preferred tree species. It was found that woodpecker cavity nest occurrence depends substantially on mature forest structure for nesting, highlighting the importance of retaining adequate amount of snags and larger trees, aligning with sustainable forest management practices. These findings emphasize community‐managed tropical sal forests as important habitats for primary cavity excavators, particularly Picidae. Our study highlights the importance of retaining large native trees, snags, and cavity‐bearing tree species in forest management plans to support woodpeckers and the larger cavity‐nesting species in South Asia.
n65a9b1de779f: Aposematic colouration in animals advertises prey toxicity and unpalatability to predators. However, intra‐specific variation in aposematic signals is widespread and often thought to be the result of environmental factors such as temperature. To investigate how temperature affects warning colour, we used the aposematic seed bug Lygaeus simulans as a model. Wild‐type adults of this species exhibit the typical red and black pattern common among many aposematic insects, while “pale” mutants are yellow and black. Here, we investigated how rearing temperatures affect their warning colour, fitness traits, and protein expression. We found that L. simulans warning colouration is temperature sensitive, with both pale‐mutant and wild‐type individuals redder at lower temperatures (24°C) compared to higher (32°C) temperatures. Reduced body size (weight and length) was also found at this lower temperature. Utilising SWATH‐proteomic analysis, we identified 15 differentially expressed proteins between the two morphs, including Glutathione S‐transferase (GST), a protein involved in oxidative states. Subsequent analysis of GST activity showed higher activity in pale‐mutants compared to wild‐types at 29°C. Furthermore, in males, this difference between morphs mirrored the colour change as it was not evident at 24°C, although this was not the case in females. Our research reveals a distinctive temperature‐dependent variation in aposematic colouration, providing a greater understanding of how warning signals evolve with temperature changes.
n347227542951: The endangered Australian sea lion (Neophoca cinerea) divides its functional ecology between land (for mating and pup-rearing) and sea (for foraging). Given this amphibious lifestyle, it is susceptible to natural and anthropogenic sound exposure in both air and water. Hearing data for the species are limited to a small sample size (two individuals) of behavioural measurements in air at only a few frequencies, and no underwater hearing thresholds are currently available. Understanding its auditory sensitivity is important for assessing potential risks from anthropogenic sound across its habitat. This study used computed tomography-based finite-element modelling of three post-mortem Australian sea lion heads to simulate frequency-dependent sound reception across broad frequency ranges in air and under water. Transfer functions were calculated as the ratio of stapes-footplate velocity to incident sound pressure, providing a quantitative measure of mechanical sound transmission to the inner ear. The models indicated differences in sound reception between the two media. The transfer functions were subsequently converted into estimated audiogram curves by anchoring the minimum thresholds to published values for Australian sea lions and closely related otariid species. The resulting curves were broadly consistent with published otariid audiograms. This study provides a mechanistic description of aerial and underwater sound reception in Australian sea lions, together with an anatomically informed basis for estimating hearing sensitivity and identifying frequency ranges relevant to anthropogenic sound exposure. More broadly, it provides the first mechanistic estimate of underwater hearing in ASLs and demonstrates the potential of CT-based finite-element modelling as a conservation physiology tool for inaccessible marine mammals.
nd3f5154c517f: The Carpathian population of the Eurasian lynx (Lynx lynx carpathicus) represents one of the most important native source populations for lynx conservation and reinforcement in Central Europe, yet ecological drivers of prey selection remain poorly understood. We investigated diet composition, and factors influencing prey selection in the Western Carpathians using an integrated approach combining GPS telemetry and systematic kill-site inspections, snow tracking, scat analysis, camera trapping and microsatellite genotyping for individual lynx identification from scats. Based on 446 prey remains and 386 scat samples collected across several mountain regions, we found that the lynx diet was overwhelmingly dominated by wild ungulates, which accounted for 96.0% of prey remains and 96.3% of total consumed biomass. Roe deer (Capreolus capreolus) was the main prey species, representing 64.6% of prey remains and 69.0% of consumed biomass, followed by red deer (Cervus elaphus; 27.6% and 24.8%, respectively). Despite substantial variation in ungulate community composition and the availability of alternative prey, roe deer remained consistently positively selected across all study areas. In contrast, red deer consumption increased with its relative availability and was more frequent in males, particularly during winter, indicating context-dependent flexibility in prey use. Non-ungulate prey contributed only marginally to the diet, and we found little evidence that lynx age, social status or population density substantially influenced prey selection. Our results demonstrate that Carpathian lynx remain strongly specialized on roe deer while retaining capacity to exploit alternative ungulate prey under specific ecological conditions. These findings improve our understanding of predator–prey interactions in a key European lynx population and provide an important scientific basis for conservation and management of lynx and its prey. Our integrated approach and findings also provide an ecological benchmark for anticipating predator–prey relationships as lynx recover across their former range through natural recolonization, reinforcement and reintroduction.
na4b485801dba: Citizen-science initiatives generate large numbers of image-supported fungal observations that can contribute to biodiversity recording, but their scientific value depends partly on reliable species identification. Recognition from field photographs is challenged by variable imaging conditions, a long-tailed species-frequency distribution, and visual similarity, while ecological descriptors recorded with the same observations provide context unavailable to image-only models. We examined whether habitat, substrate, and month improve fungal species recognition and compared matched strategies for incorporating these fields. Using Danish Fungi 2024-Mini (36,393 images from 20,618 observations of 182 species), we developed the Multi-scale Ecological Fusion Network (MEF-Net), which combines pooled multi-scale ConvNeXt descriptors with ecological descriptors through direct fusion and bounded channel recalibration. At an input resolution of 224 × 224 pixels, MEF-Net achieved mean Top-1 accuracy, Top-3 accuracy, and Macro-F1 values of 72.21%, 88.35%, and 61.68%, respectively, across five independent runs, a 5.51-percentage-point increase in Macro-F1 over the matched image-only ConvNeXt-Base model. At 384 × 384 pixels, mean Macro-F1 was 63.72%, 4.21 percentage points higher than the matched image-only model. These overall gains reflected the combined contributions of the multi-scale visual representation and ecological-context integration. Habitat produced the largest mean gain among the individual fields, whereas using all three fields jointly produced the best metadata-aware result. In the controlled strategy comparison, ecological conditioning of the pooled visual descriptors achieved the highest mean performance, while direct concatenation and calibrated Bayesian Late Fusion also improved upon the matched multi-scale image-only reference. MEF-Net achieved higher Macro-F1 across rare, medium-frequency, and frequent species, with the largest difference in the rare group. These findings indicate that ecological observation context can complement image evidence and support candidate ranking within human-validated fungal biodiversity-recording workflows.
n072ee3cb2b1a: Phthalate esters (PAEs) are widespread contaminants in freshwater ecosystems, yet how temporal shifts in congener composition relate to environmental gradients and ecological-risk patterns remains poorly understood in connected river–lake systems. In this study, 16 PAEs were investigated in 36 surface-water samples collected from 12 sites along the Mudanjiang River–Jingpo Lake system during spring, summer, and autumn 2024. Water-quality conditions and surrounding landscape pressures were also examined to evaluate the environmental context of PAE variation. Thirteen PAEs were detected, with Σ16PAEs concentrations ranging from 210.90 to 852.11 ng L−1 and averaging 513.35 ± 144.86 ng L−1. DBP was the predominant congener, accounting for 31.9% of Σ16PAEs, whereas DNP showed the highest detection frequency (86.1%). Σ16PAEs concentrations were highest in summer. The congener profile shifted from DBP dominance in spring and summer to a more even composition of DNP, DNPP, DPhP, and DNOP in autumn. PAE composition was associated with water-quality and landscape gradients, indicating that contaminant profiles varied across the observed environmental conditions. Σ16PAEs concentrations were positively associated with cumulative fish risk, but concentration dominance did not correspond directly to congener-specific risk contribution. DBP dominated the PAE burden, whereas DPhP contributed most strongly to fish risk. Non-priority PAEs also contributed substantially to both mixture composition and ecological risk. These results show that ecological-risk patterns in connected freshwater systems are shaped not only by total contaminant burden but also by temporal changes in mixture composition and environmental context. Considering congener-specific composition, non-priority contaminants, and multiple environmental pressures may therefore improve ecological-risk assessment and monitoring of river–lake ecosystems.
n4acb61a65b0b: Researchers conducted field experiments with both winter‐white and winter‐brown snowshoe hares in the Oregon Cascades to assess how these sympatric colour morphs adjust their behaviour to escape terrestrial and avian predators. While hares did not adjust their behaviour when mismatched, the researchers documented a specific technique for avoiding hawks. Abstract Shifts in predator–prey interactions in response to environmental change can affect population dynamics and community structure, but have received relatively little attention in the climate change literature. Seasonally colour‐moulting species face increased predation risk when winter‐white individuals experience camouflage mismatch in snowless conditions. While hares (genus Lepus) exhibit behavioural plasticity to reduce predation risk in other contexts, hares in populations of winter‐white individuals have demonstrated limited capacity to adjust behaviour to mitigate mismatch or its consequences. Little is known about antipredator behaviour in polymorphic populations of sympatric polyphenic winter‐white and invariant winter‐brown individuals that experience contrasting camouflage mismatch across seasons. We examined escape behaviours in a polymorphic population of snowshoe hares (Lepus americanus) including both winter‐white and winter‐brown individuals. In field experiments, we assessed plasticity in escape behaviour in response to predator type and camouflage mismatch. Using 224 measurements of concealment and flight initiation distance in 74 wild hares, we tested whether escape behaviour varied with colour morph and camouflage mismatch. We also quantified discrete escape decisions (flight, vegetation refuge or subsurface refuge) by 29 individual hares in 52 predator escape trials to test for behavioural responses to predator type (humans, hunting dogs Canis familiaris and goshawks Astur atricapillus). Linear mixed‐effects models revealed no relationship between colour morph or mismatch and either concealment or flight initiation distance, suggesting a lack of behavioural adjustment to reduce mismatch‐associated predation risk in both winter‐white and winter‐brown hares. In contrast, hares exhibited strong behavioural plasticity in response to predator type, using subsurface refuges more often in trials with avian, but not terrestrial predators. The odds of subsurface refuge use were 14.3 times higher in trials with goshawks compared to human trials. Collectively, we find that winter‐white and winter‐brown snowshoe hares exhibit predator recognition and corresponding behavioural plasticity to different predator types, but not to camouflage mismatch, highlighting limits to behavioural plasticity in response to climate‐driven increases in predation risk.
n21aca9db7b5e: Our study provides experimental evidence of the immediate physiological and behavioural costs faced by mountain lizards moving to higher elevations, integrating home range data with behavioural, physiological and body condition metrics to offer new insights into how elevation shifts constrain species' ability to cope with rapid climate change. Abstract Animals are known to move across elevations in response to climate change. However, the costs and challenges associated with these movements are not well‐understood. Therefore, it is essential to explore how animals respond to a novel elevation to comprehensively understand their strategies for mitigating the effects of climate change. In this study, we examined fitness‐related traits of the high‐elevation toad‐headed agama (Phrynocephalus vlangalii) on the Qinghai–Xizang Plateau following elevational translocation using a 2 (population origins) × 2 (elevational environments) design. We switched lizards between habitats at 2600 and 3600‐m elevation, assessing their body condition, home ranges, behavioural thermoregulation, thermal physiology, locomotor performance and resting metabolic rates at both native and translocation sites. We found that the lizards from the 3600 m a.s.l. performed equally well at both 2600‐m and 3600‐m elevation sites. In contrast, the lizards from the 2600 m a.s.l. performed well at their native elevation but struggled at the 3600‐m site, indicated by decreased accuracy and effectiveness of thermoregulation, reduced locomotion and resting metabolic rates, shrunken home ranges and a significant decline in body condition. Our study highlights the challenges and costs animals face when moving to higher elevations to escape the impacts of climate change. It also emphasizes the importance of assessing immediate responses to novel environments when evaluating the efficacy of dispersal as a buffering strategy against climate change.
n538257070fe2: Migrant frugivorous birds can partially assist fleshy‐fruited plants fruiting during spring migration to track climate change, although severe warming and land‐cover alteration may strongly constrain seed‐dispersal range filling. Importantly, range filling capacity is uneven across plant species: differences in climatically suitable ranges and intrinsic traits, particularly seed size, influence the ability of species to reach newly suitable areas.
