n29d1eae3b3ce: Across forests worldwide, frequent climate extremes and intensified timber harvest are reshaping forest structure by increasing tree mortality and canopy opening, threatening terrestrial biodiversity and ecosystem sustainability. In unmanaged forests, natural disturbances create canopy gaps and leave substantial deadwood on site, whereas timber harvesting creates gaps through the removal of living trees, thereby limiting the accumulation of deadwood. However, how these disturbances and management practices affect ecosystem functioning, especially of the belowground system, remains little understood. Here, we reconstructed 116 soil animal food webs in a full‐factorial experiment manipulating forest gaps and deadwood addition. We quantified energy fluxes of soil food webs as an integrative measure of belowground ecosystem functioning and investigated their network architecture 2 years after establishment of the experiment. Forest gaps reduced total food web energy fluxes by 13.4%, decreased network connectance, and shifted energy flow towards the bacteria‐dominated “fast” channel, indicating simplified soil food webs, impaired soil functioning, and reduced energy retention belowground. However, compared to gaps without deadwood, the presence of deadwood in gaps increased total energy flux by 37.4%, primarily through enhanced fungivory and wood‐feeding pathways, and restored network connectance and cycling rates to levels comparable to those in closed‐canopy forests. Our results demonstrate that deadwood acts as a key structural component that mitigates the detrimental effects of canopy gap formation on belowground ecosystem functioning, underscoring deadwood retention after timber harvest as a practical strategy to safeguard soil functioning in a more disturbance‐prone future.
n2cf8edd9f85d: Ocean warming, acidification, and deoxygenation, among other co‐occurring factors, are shifting species ranges throughout the marine environment. Mesophotic and deep corals are understudied in their response to climate changes, particularly in the Red Sea, which has relatively high temperatures and salinities and is projected to undergo major changes in the future, with little assessment of the impacts to date. Ecological niche modelling can be used to explain the known distribution of a species, predict its current range, and estimate future range shift under changing ocean scenarios. Here, we estimate the area of suitable habitat for four mesophotic and deep‐sea corals (Acanthogorgia spp., Stylaster tritoni, Bathypathes thermophila, and Madracis interjecta) across the whole Red Sea under present conditions and under different scenarios of future environmental changes (years 2090–2100). We found variations in the responses of these corals, but two of the four taxa are projected to lose significant amounts of their current habitats, while the other two lose a smaller portion. In particular, the scleractinian coral M. interjecta is likely to lose the largest proportion of its habitat, while the black coral B. thermophila may experience the least change. Deeper areas may become suitable for these corals, but colonisation will depend on their ability to disperse. We also assessed the potential biodiversity hotspots both now and in the future, finding the northern Red Sea to be one ecologically important area. These results enable marine spatial planning in support of an effective long‐term conservation action to protect these important habitats.
nbd77b5cd15eb: We evaluated drought‐induced damage, resistance and recovery in several Mediterranean woody species spanning contrasting regeneration strategies. By integrating hydraulic and leaf turgor safety margins, foliar damages, mortality and non‐structural carbohydrates, we identified three drought‐induced functional phases. Mortality and recovery diverged between obligate seeders and resprouters, showing that crossing physiological safety thresholds does not necessarily translate into equivalent mortality outcomes. Abstract The Mediterranean region is warming around 20% faster than the global average, and models project declines between 10% and 30% in precipitation by the middle of the century. Increasing drought and heat stress conditions are causing massive climate‐driven forest decline and mortality episodes around the world, especially exacerbated in water‐limited ecosystems. Therefore, it is critical to understand species‐specific physiological thresholds underlying drought‐induced mortality. We experimentally compare drought resistance and short‐term resilience of Mediterranean woody species with contrasting post‐disturbance regeneration strategies (obligate seeders vs. resprouters) along a controlled drought stress gradient. Our aim is to unravel the physiological mechanisms behind drought‐induced mortality and assess variations in the safety thresholds of both plant regeneration strategies. We quantify hydraulic safety margins (HSM), leaf turgor safety margins (LTSM), leaf damage, mortality and non‐structural carbohydrates (NSC). Both HSM and LTSM decline as the drought intensifies, but their relationship with mortality differs from a simple threshold avoidance pattern. Mortality increases with decreasing HSM and LTSM in both regeneration strategies. Seeders show substantially higher mortality around HSM = 0, while resprouters frequently operate beyond HSM = 0 with lower mortality. Leaf damage emerges as a strong predictor of mortality, with a more severe response in seeders, while declining NSC concentrations were associated with a marked increase in mortality in seeders, but not in resprouters. Our results reinforce current mortality models that invoke dual thresholds, loss of stem conductivity and safety margins, and carbohydrate depletion as decisive predictors of drought‐induced mortality in plants. Synthesis. Our findings present key insights into the role of plant regeneration strategy and physiological characteristics in enhancing resilience to drought and identify different drought‐induced functional phases defined by the interaction between HSM and LTSM. These results emphasize the importance of promoting mixed communities of these co‐occurring strategies in the conservation and adaptive management plans of Mediterranean forest ecosystems in the context of global change. L'augment de les condicions de sequera i estrès tèrmic està provocant episodis massius de declivi i mortalitat forestal induïts pel clima a tot el món, situació especialment agreujada en ecosistemes amb limitacions hídriques. Per això, resulta fonamental comprendre els llindars fisiològics específics de cada espècie que estan subjacent a la mortalitat induïda per la sequera. n2e14074c7d5b: Two large‐scale field surveys, a dry decade apart, show decreases in woody vegetation cover, particularly in drier Mediterranean regions. However, species diversity provides critical resilience. Plant communities with high species richness‐maintained stability, effectively buffering drought impacts and preventing vegetation loss. Abstract Changes in temperature, rainfall regimes and water availability, as part of global climate change, lead to increased drought stress, especially in dry ecosystems. Yet empirical evidence of how woody vegetation responds to such climate drying remains scarce. We examined changes in woody cover and species composition across 71 woodland and shrubland sites, spanning the east Mediterranean climatic gradient, resurveyed a decade apart (2008–2009 and 2018–2019). The studied decade was characterized by reduced rainfall and a shorter rainy season combined with consistent warming, resulting in increasing aridity. Woody cover declined in 52% of sites and increased in 24% of them. The magnitude of decline was greatest in arid regions and was strongly predicted by mean annual precipitation. Model selection identified species richness as a stabilizing factor: sites with high species richness experienced smaller losses or maintained stable woody cover. At the species level, we identified seven dominant tree, shrub and sub‐shrub species. Of these, Quercus coccifera var. calliprinos showed consistent increases in cover, correlated with the rainfall gradient, whereas the cover of Pistacia lentiscus, Calicotome villosa, Cistus spp., and Sarcopoterium spinosum declined. The cover of Phillyrea latifolia and Rhamnus spp. was relatively stable. However, climatic variability explained only a small portion of the change in cover of each of the dominant species. Synthesis. Our results reveal a shift from the well‐documented trajectory of secondary woodland regeneration towards regional declines in woody cover under intensifying aridity. Our findings provide rare field‐based evidence that species richness enhances vegetation resistance to climate drying. תקופת יובש ממושכתאחר דעיכת הצומח המעוצה ל שינויים בטמפרטורה, במשטר הגשמים ובזמינות המים כחלק משינוי האקלים העולמי מובילים לעלייה בעקת יובש לצמחים במיוחד במערכות אקולוגיות יובשניות. עם זאת, עדויות אמפיריות לגבי האופן שבו צמחייה מעוצה מגיבה לעלייה בעקת יובש כזו נותרו מועטות. של מזרח הים התיכון, אשר נסקרו פעמיים בהפרש של עשור (2008–2009 ו‐2018–2019). העשור שנחקר אופיין בירידה בכמות הגשמים ובהתקצרות עונת הגשמים, בשילוב עם התחממות עקבית, מה שהוביל לעלייה ביובשנות. במחקר זה בחנו שינויים בכיסוי המעוצה ובהרכב המינים ב‐71 אתרי צומח טבעי ‐ חורשים, שיחיות ובתות, המשתרעים לאורך המפל האקלימי הכיסוי המעוצה ירד ב‐52% מהאתרים ועלה ב‐24% מהם. עוצמת הירידה הייתה הגדולה ביותר באזורים היבשים יחסית ונמצאה קשורה לכמות המשקעים השנתית הממוצעת. עושר המינים נמצא כגורם מייצב: השינוי בכיסוי הצומח היה קטן יותר או נשמר יציב באתרים בעלי עושר מינים גבוה. שעיר ומרווני, וסירה קוצנית ירד ברוב האתרים. הכיסוי של בר‐זית בינוני הראה עלייה כללית בכיסוי ומתאם למפל הגשם בעוד שהכיסוי של המינים אלת המסטיק, קידה שעירה, לוטם ברמת המין, זיהינו שבעה מיני עצים, שיחים ובני‐שיח דומיננטיים. מתוכם, האלון המצוי היה יציב יחסית. עם זאת, השונות האקלימית הסבירה רק חלק קטן מהשינוי בכיסוי של כל אחד מהמינים הדומיננטיים ואשחר א"י ונקוד. סינתזה :תוצאותינו חושפות תפנית מהמסלול המתועד היטב של סוקציה משנית לעבר דעיכה בכיסוי המעוצה עקב התגברות היובשנות. בנוסף, ממצאינו מספקים עדות נדירה מן השדה לכך שעושר מינים מגביר את עמידות הצמחייה לתהליך העלייה ביובשנות.
nc7aedf720e4b: Proposed model for the regulatory network of FveJAG governing leaf shape in woodland strawberry. Summary Leaves play a vital role in photosynthesis, respiration, and transpiration, significantly impacting a plant's adaptability and crop yield. Strawberry plants develop trifoliate compound leaves, the molecular regulatory pathways of which are not well‐understood. Here, we identified a woodland strawberry (Fragaria vesca) mutant, designated simple leaf 2 (sl2), which exhibits the complete suppression of the two lateral leaflets. The causal gene encodes a C2H2 zinc‐finger transcription factor that is homologous to JAGGED and is named FveJAG. A point mutation located within the intron triggers alternative splicing and generates a premature stop codon. The prior key transcriptional regulator of leaflet initiation, SIMPLE LEAF1 (SL1), directly targets the promoter of FveJAG to activate its transcription. The synergistic interaction between sl1 and sl2 indicates that SL1 and FveJAG function within the same regulatory pathway. Genetic and expression analyses suggest that FveJAG also acts downstream of FveMYB117a during leaflet initiation. Taken together, our results uncover a direct SL1 target gene and elucidate a complex regulatory network involving SL1, FveJAG, and FveMYB117a in strawberry compound leaf morphogenesis, offering further mechanistic insights into the genetic regulation of leaf complexity.
n2216b7d349ab: System architecture of PGCopilot. The system architecture comprises four layers: (1) data sources, including locally built resources (Botanical Knowledge Base using ChromaDB and Qwen3‐embedding; Multi‐Database Resources with 1.83 M records across seven plant species) and runtime‐accessed external resources (PubMed via NCBI E‐utilities); (2) an MCP Tool Layer with 31 specialized tools built on the FastMCP framework, including locally developed tools implemented with FastMCP and the official STRING MCP service; (3) PGCopilot Core integrating prompt governance, LLM reasoning engine (DeepSeek‐V3.2), and evidence integration modules; and (4) a Query & Response Interface providing entity grounding, ID mapping, multi‐database retrieval, and conflict reporting. Summary The exponential expansion of multi‐omic data presents a major bottleneck for researchers seeking to derive biological insights from heterogeneous genomic resources. Although large language models (LLMs) enable natural language interaction with scientific knowledge, general‐purpose LLMs are not designed to reason over plant‐specific biological issues and frequently produce hallucinated or oversimplified outputs. We developed PGCopilot, an AI‐assisted research agent tailored for plant functional genomics. It integrated task planning, identifier disambiguation, and tool orchestration to actively retrieve and synthesize evidence across heterogeneous biological databases using the Model Context Protocol. Built on a knowledge base of 1.83 million records, together with online access to PubMed titles and available abstracts covering over 33 million indexed articles and STRING protein–protein interaction data, it could plan retrieval strategies and integrate evidence into grounded responses, reducing unsupported outputs and addressing data fragmentation and identifier discrepancies. In expert‐guided benchmarking, PGCopilot achieved higher performance than the evaluated baseline LLMs, demonstrating advantages in task relevance, evidence integration, hallucination control, and research utility, and providing more verifiable citations and explicit reporting of cross‐database inconsistencies. As an autonomous agent supporting multiturn tool interaction, it streamlined cross‐database evidence integration from labor‐intensive search‐and‐retrieval to automated analysis‐and‐synthesis. This approach streamlines cross‐database navigation and evidence integration, allowing researchers to focus more on hypothesis formulation, experimental design, and critical interpretation of comprehensive evidence.
n82ed6f6eb34c: Alignment between biologically meaningful units and stock boundaries is one or the requirements for sustainable resource management. In Norway, harbour seals (Phoca vitulina vitulina) are managed at the county level and, when local populations are deemed sufficiently large to support harvesting, hunting is permitted under a quota corresponding to 5% of the counted individuals. An assessment of population structure along the entire Norwegian coastline based upon 16 microsatellites revealed significant overall differentiation (F ST = 0.036, p < 0.001) consistent with a pattern of Isolation by Distance, in agreement with the estimated effective migration surface (EEMS). Pairwise differentiation among sampling sites challenged the current stock outline. Specifically, (a) geographically large counties (e.g., Finnmark, Nordland) could warrant subdivision into smaller management units, whereas (b) no differentiation was detected across the four south-eastern counties (Agder, Vestfold, Telemark and Østfold). Positive and statistically significant spatial autocorrelation detected at distances of 0–300 km invoked larger genetical similarity than expected by chance and agreed with the fine-grained population structure revealed by former tagging studies. The absence of evidence for recent bottleneck events suggests that populations remain at mutation-drift equilibrium.
n8814f99cbe0e: Biological invasions are intensifying worldwide as a major component of global change, with soil microbes increasingly recognized as key regulators of invasion outcomes. Yet how soil microbes interact with biodiversity to determine whether communities resist or facilitate invasion, particularly through their effects on plant growth and species interactions, remains unclear. Here, we conducted a two‐phase feedback experiment in which soils were conditioned across a diversity gradient of native or invasive plant communities. We characterized soil fungal communities and quantified microbial effects on plant growth and species interactions between phylogenetically paired native and invasive species. Biodiversity generated contrasting invasion outcomes depending on community origin, driven by distinct microbial pathways. In native‐conditioned soils, increasing diversity reduced invader dominance (biotic resistance), primarily mediated by microbial effects on interspecific competition that enhanced native competition strength while reducing that of invaders. In contrast, in invasive‐conditioned soils, increasing diversity facilitated invader dominance (invasional meltdown), primarily driven by enhanced invader growth and suppression of natives. These patterns were associated with shifts in key microbial groups. Putative pathogen richness increased with increasing plant diversity and was negatively associated with native growth, whereas AMF richness declined with increasing plant diversity in native communities but increased with increasing plant diversity in invasive communities, promoting invader growth and competition strength. By integrating biodiversity‐ecosystem functioning, biotic resistance, invasional meltdown, and competitive interactions within a plant–soil feedback framework, our study advances invasion ecology. It identifies soil microbes as central mediators that link biodiversity to ecosystem invasibility through distinct pathways affecting plant growth and species interactions.
n19a96c3d6957: In a desert‐steppe biodiversity experiment, legume biomass proportion was associated mainly with leaf‐trait reorganization, whereas species richness showed more consistent associations with nematode faunal indices and footprint metrics. Measured leaf traits differed in predictive importance between herbivore feeding guilds. Positive associations between piercing‐sucking insect abundance and selected nematode indicators suggested a potential connection between above‐ground and below‐ground communities. Abstract Plant functional composition and species richness may be associated with different aspects of above‐ and below‐ground communities. Distinguishing these relationships is important for understanding how biodiversity‐related patterns extend across trophic levels. However, their respective associations with plant traits, herbivore feeding guilds and below‐ground food webs remain unclear in resource‐limited desert steppes. We sampled 64 plots during the fourth growing season of a desert‐steppe biodiversity experiment. We examined associations of realized legume biomass proportion and plant species richness with community‐weighted plant traits, chewing and piercing‐sucking herbivores, and nematode faunal indices and footprint metrics derived from relative sequence composition. Analyses combined joint regressions, direct feeding‐guild comparisons, random‐forest analyses and theory‐informed piecewise structural equation modelling. Higher legume biomass proportion was associated with lower community‐weighted leaf mass per area and higher density‐normalized leaf punch strength and trichome density. Several plant traits showed relatively high predictive importance for chewing insects but consistently low importance for piercing‐sucking insects. However, the direct mixed‐effects comparison did not detect a significant difference between guild‐specific responses to legume biomass proportion. Plant species richness was positively associated with the nematode structure and enrichment indices and negatively associated with the composite footprint metric (MF), whereas legume biomass proportion showed no significant conditional associations with these measures. Piercing‐sucking insect abundance was positively correlated with the herbivore footprint metric after multiple‐testing correction and showed positive conditional associations with the nematode structure index and MF in the piecewise SEM. Synthesis. Legume biomass proportion was linked primarily to above‐ground leaf‐trait reorganization, whereas plant species richness showed more consistent associations with below‐ground nematode faunal organization. Piercing‐sucking insect abundance showed positive associations with the nematode structure index and the composite and herbivore footprint metrics, suggesting a potential cross‐realm connection involving this feeding guild. Together, these findings indicate that plant functional composition, species richness and consumer feeding guilds represent different but connected dimensions of multitrophic organization in resource‐limited grasslands.
nb19b1f26bf0b: The evolution of the amniote genome is characterized by a striking dichotomy between extreme karyotypic stasis and rapid structural innovation. To identify the mechanisms governing this variation, we provide a comprehensive synthesis of chromosome number and karyotype data across non‐avian reptiles, birds and mammals, integrating a century of classical cytogenetics with modern chromosome‐scale genomics. Amniote chromosome numbers span a range from 2n = 6 to 142 and have been shaped primarily by chromosomal fusions and fissions rather than by polyploidization common in non‐amniotes. Recent ancestral state reconstructions suggest a highly fragmented ancestral amniote karyotype of 2n = 88 with a bipartite organization of macro‐ and microchromosomes. They also support environmental sex determination as the plesiomorphic state. We explore the evolutionary mechanisms facilitating chromosomal turnover, including lineage‐specific transposable element activity, hybridization‐driven genomic instability and genetic hitchhiking, alongside the canalization model and the position‐effect hypothesis as primary responses to environmental transitions. Social structure, such as polygynous harem systems, can further contribute to rearrangement fixation via genetic drift in some, but not all, lineages. Chromosomal divergence across these lineages serves as a useful cytotaxonomic marker and, in some cases, a barrier to gene flow, as in the postzygotic incompatibility of equid and cervid hybrids. In contrast, introgression persists across karyotypically divergent rock‐wallabies and crocodilians, indicating that the reproductive consequences of karyotypic divergence are lineage‐specific rather than a fixed function of karyotypic distance. This synthesis presents an updated atlas of amniote chromosomal evolution and provides a conceptual framework for understanding how molecular mechanisms, ecological shifts and behavioural factors interact to shape genomic structure.
n2e363e6da541: Understanding genetic diversity and structure in natural populations is important for conservation and developing resilience into restored populations for the future. Populations at the lower latitude (or northern) range edges tend to have lower levels of genetic diversity and are poorly connected, although they may be locally adapted to warmer environments. The temperate seagrass, Posidonia sinuosa, occurs across a latitudinal gradient along the Western Australian coastline. Some meadows have experienced significant decline due to industrialisation and urbanisation of coastal areas. We investigated spatial genetic diversity, structure, and local adaptation using single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). All meadows had similarly low levels of genetic diversity with high levels of inbreeding, despite high clonal diversity. Weak genetic structure was consistent with genetic connectivity, enabled by sea‐surface seed dispersal. Approximately 6.1% of SNPs were identified as putatively adaptive and most were associated with temperature variables. Allelic turnover was associated with < 1.4°C temperature change, suggesting plants may be sensitive to small temperature changes. Meadows are currently growing in temperatures below their thermal optima, so may tolerate future projected temperatures up to a point. Importantly, this temperature increase is below the 1.5°C–2.0°C goal of the Paris Agreement and plants are unlikely to tolerate current projections for 2100, which equate to +3.2°C, in addition to extreme heatwave events. Conservation of fragmented, northern, warmer‐adapted meadows will be important to assist recovery and persistence of damaged meadows into the future, as translocation of putatively warmer‐adapted genotypes that have exhibited historic connectivity may be a viable strategy for restoration of impacted higher latitude meadows.
n8f2a9ec15b5c: With prodigious biomass and diversity, herbivorous insects are among the world's most successful animals. It is widely believed, however, that some plant‐based diets do not meet the needs of insect metabolism. Microbial symbionts may balance such deficits through diverse biochemistry. Here, we consider whether obligate nutritional symbioses between insects and microbes support large portions of insect herbivore diversity. In doing so, we assess the evidence that these highly integrated relationships are key innovations, circumventing nutritive shortfalls within particular plant tissues. Toward these ends, we compile nutrient data for 20 plant‐ and non‐plant foods, plus data on diet and symbiosis across 874 families of insects—both herbivorous and non‐herbivorous. Our results reinforce widely believed, but often uncited evidence that several insect taxa have long‐consumed plant tissues with low concentrations of B‐vitamins, nitrogen, or accessible carbon. Emerging as symbiont‐enriched are seed‐feeders, which face insufficient quantities of several B‐vitamins in their food. Experimental and genome assessments show how symbionts surmount these B‐vitamin shortcomings, showing also where this same challenge, and those of high fibre or low amino acid content are surmounted through symbiosis on other diets. We thus show where symbiont services are key innovations. Over half of the world's insect herbivores persist without nutritive assistance from obligate symbionts. This is largely because many consume leaves, which are reasonably good sources of amino acids and B‐vitamins. Lateral transfer of microbial genes encoding plant cell‐wall degrading enzymes has helped to overcome high fibre content, defusing the most challenging nutritive aspect of leaf‐chewing diets.
n5f864ffb6561: In 2012, one of us observed an adult male peninsula dragon (Ctenophorus fionni) predate a juvenile conspecific. This was noteworthy as we understood peninsula dragons to be primarily insectivorous and it prompted us to investigate cannibalism more generally using a systematic, comprehensive review of the literature. Cannibalism has never been reported in any wild, natural‐living Australo‐Papuan (i.e., Amphibolurine) agamid, except in the peninsula dragon. There are now three records of cannibalism in the peninsula dragon, all from populations of the central form. This raises the possibility that peninsula dragons, or certain populations thereof, may be unusually predisposed to cannibalism. However, the current data available are too sparse to draw firm conclusions and we encourage anyone with observations of cannibalism to publish them.
nfa007b29627b: Microbiomes play crucial roles in ecosystems, largely through their interactions with plants. Fungal endophytes occur in nearly all plant tissues and can influence host physiology, stress tolerance, and productivity. Although previous studies have examined how air temperature shapes foliar endophyte communities, endophytes may respond more strongly to leaf temperatures, which are often decoupled from ambient air temperatures. Consequently, changes in leaf temperature (e.g., due to global warming) may alter endophyte diversity and composition. In this study, we experimentally tested whether elevated leaf temperatures affect fungal endophyte richness and community composition in six native subtropical plant species from South Florida. Using in situ localized heating of individual branches, we increased leaf temperatures by 1°C–3°C over a 2‐week period. Leaf thermal profiles were monitored with thermal imaging, and pre‐ and post‐treatment leaf samples were collected from warmed and control branches for fungal DNA extraction, ITS sequencing, and community analysis. Our results show that fungal leaf endophyte richness and composition were strongly determined by host plant identity, but were unaffected by warming. Linear mixed‐effects models and paired t‐tests showed no significant changes in ESV richness with heating across all hosts. Similarly, distance‐based redundancy analysis and PERMANOVA tests revealed no significant shifts in fungal community composition due to increased leaf temperatures. However, a random forest classification model identified a subset of fungal ESV that were predictive of temperature treatment. While overall endophyte communities were stable, specific taxa may be thermally responsive. Foliar fungal endophyte communities in subtropical woody plants may be resistant to short‐term warming. Such stability could buffer host plants against microbial disruption during temperature extremes, though it may also limit adaptive microbial turnover. This study advances understanding of plant–microbe thermal dynamics and underscores the need for further research on the functional resistance of endophyte communities under climate change.
nd72f745c8d07: Long‐term individual‐based studies have invaluably advanced our understanding of animal ecology and evolution. Participants involved in the creation and/or maintenance of long‐term study systems benefit from synergistic collaborations, which can provide greater opportunities for co‐authorship. We conducted two surveys to collect anonymous data from current and former participants of long‐term individual‐based studies about leadership structure and authorship patterns as it is unclear whether all participants—regardless of their intersectional identity—derive the same benefits from participation in these systems. Our goal was to collect these data in a less harmful way through self‐reporting gender compared to gendering participants/authors by their first name. We found that gender representation was biased toward men historically and has recently become more equitable across genders. PI gender demographics were positively associated with the gender composition of project participants. Male PIs had higher numbers of publications compared to those of marginalized genders for overall authorship and as last author. Our results parallel similar patterns observed across other science disciplines. This research may serve as a first step in sparking broader reflection, discussion, and action on how gender data is collected and to ensure that the remarkable opportunities offered by long‐term individual‐based study systems are equitably accessible to all.
nfb509f027087: Novel species interactions between resident and range shifting species in response to warming are posing challenges for conservation and management. This is especially the case when major predatory species are involved, as seen in the appearance of a mixed species outbreak of coral‐eating crown‐of‐thorns sea stars Acanthaster cf. solaris (As) and the lesser‐known Acanthaster brevispinus (Ab) in the tropical to subtropical transition zone in eastern Australia. The outbreak consisted of reproductively mature animals, and we investigated the potential for cross‐species hybridisation in fertilisation experiments across a range of sperm concentrations to sperm limitation conditions (106–102 sperm mL−1). Fertilisation was successful in all combinations of parents (As ♂ × As ♀, Ab ♂ × Ab ♀, Ab ♀ × As ♂, As ♀ × Ab ♂) with successful hybrid crosses in sperm dilutions as low as 102 sperm ml−1. Development in conspecific and heterospecific crosses was similar through the bipinnaria and brachiolaria larval stages to the juvenile. Juvenile hybrids had typical juvenile Acanthaster spp. development with a stellate five‐armed profile post metamorphosis, gaining arms after ~78 days. At no stage did the juvenile hybrids develop the distinctive pink colour trait that is characteristic of Acanthaster cf. solaris juveniles. Our results indicate that hybridisation is not restricted by sperm limitation conditions, with subsequent development of hybrids to the advanced juvenile stage. Our results highlight the potential for hybridisation and species introgression when range shifting species overlap with sister taxa. This may facilitate further range expansion or development of resilient hybrid progeny as a risk to vulnerable high latitude coral communities.
n4eab304a8b62: The bait polychaete Diopatra aciculata is commercially farmed in Australia and is collected as bait in several South African estuaries. Despite its widespread use, the species' geographic origin remains uncertain, hindering management efforts within sensitive estuarine ecosystems. Mitochondrial Cytochrome Oxidase subunit I (mtCOI) data and ddRAD‐generated single‐nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were used to gain insight into the origin and genetic diversity of D. aciculata. A total of 204 individuals were collected from an aquaculture farm in Australia and the Knysna, Keurbooms, and Swartkops Estuaries in South Africa. The mtCOI analyses supported the monophyly of D. aciculata and revealed lower genetic diversity in the South African population compared to the Australian population. Both marker sets revealed significant genetic differentiation between the continental populations that are naturally isolated by the Indian Ocean basin. The SNP dataset revealed low intrapopulation genetic diversity for both the Australian and South African populations. The discordant genetic diversity findings between the mtCOI and SNP datasets may be attributed to the differences in the evolutionary rate of the two marker systems. In addition, the low genomic diversity observed in the SNP dataset is consistent with the effects of captive breeding in the Australian aquaculture population; consequently, the effect of sampling bias cannot be excluded. However, the mtCOI signal of reduced diversity in South Africa is consistent with an introduced population and both mtCOI and SNP‐based RASP analyses recovered Australian samples in a basal position, suggesting Australia as the plausible origin. This highlights the need for precautionary conservation efforts to prevent further spread.
n6b2c450f2ae5: Although citizen science is increasingly used in biodiversity monitoring, moving beyond passive observation toward the active collection of high-quality biological samples remains a major challenge. To address this, we present a participatory framework originating as a bottom-up initiative, designed to facilitate the active and structured collection of high-quality biological samples. This conceptual framework allows for the development of a genuine partnership where collective field expertise enriches scientific data interpretation to inform conservation policy. Designed to be adapted to a wide range of conservation projects, this participatory framework is particularly effective for monitoring threatened, low-density and cryptic species across large landscapes by combining robust biological sampling with strong social engagement. We illustrate the operational strength of this framework through an eight-year case study mobilizing a network of 274 volunteers trained to collect non-invasive samples from the Eurasian lynx (Lynx lynx) in France, 42 untrained volunteers and a scat-detection dog. The sampling expanded across 13 departments, with the network collecting 729 scats with a 45.8% genetic confirmation rate. An anonymous online survey evaluating the human dimensions of the framework showed that despite baseline knowledge, most respondents reported gaining new insights and naturalist skills. Direct contribution to conservation was the primary motivation, and participation strengthened trust in science and data governance. Relationships with project coordinators drove long-term engagement, resulting in high willingness to re-engage in future projects. By co-constructing the research project with civil society from the outset, this framework bridges scientific expertise and local knowledge, addresses critical gaps in our understanding of the genetic health of an elusive species, and strengthens public ownership, social acceptance and scientific credibility of the findings, all of which are essential for successful conservation.
n95eacbdcf026: Benthic macroinvertebrates are widely used as indicators of freshwater ecosystem changes due to their sensitivity to environmental disturbance and important ecological functions. However, long-term variations in multiple biodiversity dimensions of benthic communities under eutrophication and seasonal environmental stress remain poorly understood. In this study, quarterly surveys were conducted at eight sites in Lake Chaohu from 2018 to 2024 to investigate temporal dynamics of benthic macroinvertebrate communities and their environmental drivers. A total of 33 taxa were identified, with communities consistently dominated by oligochaetes and chironomids. Density and biomass varied significantly among years and quarters, whereas species richness showed significant quarterly variation and a Year × Quarter interaction but no significant main effect of Year. Community structure Mixed-effects models further identified associations between selected. The dbRDA model explained 11.59% of the variation in biodiversity indices (R2 = 0.116, P = 0.0007), with NH4+-N, CODCr, and TN identified as significant predictors among the measured water-column variables. Mixed-effects models revealed additional associations with composite biodiversity scores, although the statistical support for some relationships was sensitive to the omission of individual observations or sites. Temporal changes were reflected mainly in community composition, functional diversity, and taxonomic distinctness rather than interannual differences in species richness. These findings support integrating multiple biodiversity dimensions into the ecological assessment of eutrophic shallow lakes.
n7bcb91fbbe78: Seed mass is a key life‐history trait that influences dispersal, seedling establishment, and plant fitness, yet its long‐term response to climate change remains poorly understood. We used two long‐term datasets of European beech (Fagus sylvatica) from the United Kingdom (1989–2024) and the Netherlands (1976–2024) to test whether seed mass has changed over time and whether any decline can be attributed to changing climate or altered resource dynamics. Seed mass declined by 13% over the study period, with a non‐linear decrease starting in the mid‐2000s. Models of year‐to‐year variation showed that seeds were smaller in years with lower reconstructed stored resources and in years that early summer was dry. Temporal contribution analysis indicated that the long‐term decline in seed mass was driven primarily by declining resource availability, with increasing drought making an additional contribution. Climate warming affects seed size in beech by direct effects of drought on seed development, and indirectly by altering reproductive dynamics and shortening the intervals available for resource recovery between reproductive events. Because seed mass influences dispersal and survival of seeds and seedlings, declines in seed mass are likely to reduce regeneration potential. Our findings identify an indirect pathway by which climate change may weaken forest regeneration.
ne137867d7bb3: Winter snowfall is a critical water source sustaining the survival and ecological functioning of biocrusts in desert ecosystems, yet how different biocrust types respond to altered snow‐depth conditions and maintain soil multifunctionality (SMF) through microbial community adjustments and life‐history strategies remains poorly understood. Based on a field snow‐manipulation experiment, we compared SMF responses in cyanobacterial and lichen crusts under snow removal, ambient snow, and double‐snow treatments across different treatment‐duration categories and further explored the underlying microbial regulatory mechanisms. Cyanobacterial and lichen crusts exhibited contrasting SMF responses to altered snow conditions. SMF significantly increased in cyanobacterial crusts in the short‐term treatment plots (1 year), whereas lichen crusts showed a significant decline only under short‐term snow removal. In the medium‐ and long‐term treatment plots (8 and 11 years), differences in SMF between altered‐snow and ambient‐snow conditions were reduced for both biocrust types. Lichen crusts mainly showed increases in bacterial and total microbial diversity under snow manipulation, whereas significant diversity responses in cyanobacterial crusts were primarily associated with fungi. Microbial life‐history strategies showed clear but biocrust‐type‐specific associations with SMF. Random forest and structural equation modeling (SEM) analyses indicated that SMF in cyanobacterial crusts was strongly constrained by the S strategy, while Y‐related metabolic pathways were positively associated with SMF; in contrast, SMF in lichen crusts was positively associated with the A strategy but negatively associated with the S strategy. Soil physicochemical properties also played an important role in regulating SMF, but their effects and interactions with microbial attributes differed between the two biocrust types. Overall, this study demonstrates that altered snow conditions regulate biocrust SMF through the coupling of soil environmental changes and microbial functional responses, with the underlying regulatory pathways strongly dependent on biocrust type.
n8cb64de4e20b: Strategically deploying acoustic telemetry receiver arrays is vital for tracking the movements of aquatic animals. Nevertheless, there is a lack of tools that provide the capacity to evaluate how well arrays perform in their study area, as well as ways to optimise receiver configurations to best meet study goals. Receiver configurations vary based on the species or behaviours being studied, environmental conditions affecting detectability or the spatial resolution being targeted (e.g. fine‐scale positioning), among other factors. Therefore, optimising detectability of transmitters across receivers—relative to the diverse study objectives that often exist—should be a major priority in acoustic telemetry research. Here, we introduce a simple probabilistic approach through an R package (arrayplanR) to plan and evaluate the detection performances of acoustic telemetry arrays, when combined with user range detection data, specifically with the goal to optimise receiver locations depending on the needs of the study (e.g. transmissions detected on n receivers, largest area covered beyond a detection probability threshold, highest detection probability across entire study area). There are two distinct workflows associated with our approach: (1) ‘DE_array_quantify’ quantifies array performance for receivers at pre‐designated locations (e.g. an existing study); and (2) ‘DE_array_optimize_1overlap’ and ‘DE_array_optimize_3overlap’ enable users to iteratively identify optimal receiver locations based on animal transmissions being detected by one receiver (e.g. planning for a broad‐scale presence study) or detected by more than one receiver (e.g. planning for a fine‐scale positioning study), respectively. Each workflow incorporates several input parameters to allow customisation based on study goals (e.g. number of receivers, minimum distance between receivers, fixed receiver location(s), anticipated animal‐receiver depth differences, habitat‐specific receiver locations). Using a simple case study, we show how optimal receiver configurations vary based on study parameters and highlight how strategic receiver deployments across different habitats or areas can improve detection capacity for telemetry studies. Overall, this work can contribute to better research planning and study design across the global telemetry community and marine, estuarine and freshwater environments.
ncb84e6f6b021: Copy number variation (CNV) constitutes a major source of adaptive genetic variation, yet its relative contribution to climate adaptation compared to non‐CNV (single‐copy) variants remains unresolved. Using whole‐genome sequencing of 125 Nelumbo nucifera (sacred lotus, a common aquatic vegetable) wild accessions spanning tropical‐temperate gradients, we distinguished 388,600 CNV‐derived SNPs from 485,982 SNPs of single‐copy regions. Latent factor mixed models (LFMM) revealed that CNV‐SNPs appear to drive adaptation to temperature extremes and precipitation seasonality, whereas non‐CNV SNPs dominate humid thermal adaptation. NnPAL2, a homologue of a drought‐related gene in Arabidopsis, shows a recent selective sweep in temperate N. nucifera, with reduced copy number and expression associated with lower precipitation in the warmest quarter. Our results suggest that CNV SNPs and non‐CNV SNPs contribute to distinct environmental axes, but the heterogeneous CNV effects across bioclimatic variables largely reflect ecotype‐specific copy number backgrounds rather than intrinsic differences in selective pressures. CNV therefore plays a disproportionate role in coping with abiotic extremes. Discriminating CNV‐derived SNPs from those derived from single‐copy genomic regions is essential for accurately understanding the genetic basis of climate adaptation, with potential applications for crop improvement.
ncc1b7b6951ba: Over 14,900 COI DNA sequences of drosophilids were used to build a character‐based diagnostic system for the identification of genera and species in the group. This approach uses aligned COI sequence characters, k‐mer characters and applies a hybrid approach that combines the two. To assess the efficacy of the diagnostics, accuracy versus coverage plots were used and resulted in the observation that practical rules (allowing 5% leakage [misidentified assignments]) perform much better than strict rules (no leakage). In addition, k = 10 was determined as the optimal k value for k‐mer character analysis. Hybrid methods incorporating both k‐mer characters and aligned DNA sequence characters outperform the individual approaches. Finally, unnamed drosophilid accessions were compiled and tentatively assigned taxonomy based on the diagnostic system developed here.
nd2998e8e2404: Iron and zinc distribution in wild‐type and transgenic Cavendish banana (Musa spp.) lines. Summary Iron deficiency remains a major public health problem in East Africa, where banana is a staple food for > 30 million people. This study investigated whether genetic modification could produce banana fruit containing nutritionally significant concentrations of iron while maintaining agronomic performance under field conditions. Six transgenes associated with iron homeostasis were expressed singly or in combination in Cavendish and Lady Finger bananas. In total, 450 genetically modified plants were field evaluated in Australia and fruit mineral concentrations assessed in the first planting crop. Elevated fruit iron and zinc concentrations, reaching 45.5 and 51.9 mg kg−1 dry weight, respectively, were associated with increased nicotianamine (NA) accumulation following expression of OsNAS. Iron concentrations sufficient to meet 50% of the estimated average requirement for children were achieved in 28 lines, with elevated NA suggesting improved iron bioavailability. Increased mineral accumulation negatively correlated with yield; however, this effect was partly mitigated by co‐expression of OsVIT1. Early indicators of yield penalty included low corm iron, high leaf zinc concentrations and reduced photosynthetic efficiency. These findings demonstrate the potential of using genetic modification for the mineral biofortification of bananas in East Africa while highlighting factors that may assist in the early identification of high‐performing biofortified lines.
nef954ec28351: PhYAB4–PhAGL6‐2 regulatory module controls lip‐related organ curvature in Paphiopedilum henryanum. Summary The orchid lip is a highly specialized floral organ that contributes to floral architecture and pollinator interaction. However, the developmental and molecular mechanisms underlying lip‐related organ curvature in Paphiopedilum remain poorly understood. Using Paphiopedilum henryanum and its Type A peloric mutant, we found that visible divergence between wild‐type petals and mutant lip‐like petals begins at Stage 4. Curvature was associated with adaxial–abaxial epidermal cell number imbalance in the distal region, whereas average epidermal cell area remained largely unchanged. Transcriptome and expression analyses identified PhAGL6‐2 as a lip‐associated AGL6 homolog enriched in lips and lip‐like petals during Stages 4–5. PhAGL6‐2 was preferentially expressed on the abaxial side, particularly in regions associated with curvature. Virus‐induced gene silencing‐mediated silencing of PhAGL6‐2 in Dendrobium Chao Praya Smile and P. henryanum affected perianth organ curvature, suggesting a broader role in floral organ morphogenesis. The YABBY transcription factor PhYAB4 directly bound the AGTGTG motif in the PhAGL6‐2 promoter and activated its transcription. Silencing PhYAB4 reduced PhAGL6‐2 expression and caused stronger floral curvature, lip outgrowths, and partial disruption of floral symmetry. These findings identify a PhYAB4–PhAGL6‐2 pathway associated with epidermal cell number imbalance and lip‐related organ curvature.
n9a0c670d75e9: Working model of the CitRWP–CsWUS regulatory axis in association with chromatin remodeling in citrus. Summary Plant regeneration underpins crop genetic improvement, yet its regulatory mechanism remains poorly characterized in woody fruit trees. The RWP‐RK domain‐containing (RKD) transcription factor CitRWP acts as a pleiotropic regulator of nucellar polyembryony and somatic embryogenesis (SE) in citrus, but its downstream molecular network remains elusive. We demonstrate that CsWUS, a core stem cell regulator, is a direct downstream target of CitRWP. CitRWP binds to the CsWUS promoter to activate its transcription. Additionally, CitRWP interacts with the SWItch/Sucrose Non‐Fermentable (SWI/SNF) chromatin‐remodeling ATPase SPLAYED (SYD), synergistically enhancing CsWUS activation, while chromatin accessibility at the CsWUS locus is enhanced upon CitRWP overexpression. We further uncover that CsWUS negatively regulates CitRWP expression via a feedback loop. CsWUS overexpression promotes SE in recalcitrant citrus callus, but causes abnormal meristem proliferation and impairs shoot organogenesis from epicotyl segments. CsWUS greatly enhanced in planta transformation efficiency in the model citrus. This study establishes the CitRWP–CsWUS regulatory axis as a central module that coordinates multiple developmental fate transitions in association with chromatin remodeling, providing novel insights into the mechanisms of cellular totipotency and plant regeneration.
n01e93e185338: Global biodiversity information suffers from gaps, biases, and uncertainty over time and space, afflicting all taxonomic groups. Incomplete or biased data introduce uncertainty into models of biodiversity trends, potentially generating faulty inferences with knock-on effects for conservation. We revisit how the limitations of biodiversity knowledge are conceptualised, expanding the current classification to encompass eleven major shortfalls spanning taxonomic, ecological, evolutionary, and biocultural aspects, and examine the impediments that limit progress in reducing them. Information gaps have been moulded by our capacity and willingness to collect data, which are constrained by a series of financial, taxonomic, and technological impediments that vary across regions and taxa. Addressing these challenges is crucial for understanding biodiversity patterns and processes and developing effective conservation actions.
n761f3c446954: Molecular sexing is a widely used approach for identifying the sex of monomorphic birds, but existing primers often target relatively large products that are difficult to amplify from highly degraded DNA. In this study, we developed a new primer set (voEP_F/voEP_R/P2) based on allele‐specific polymerase chain reaction (ASPCR) to facilitate the sexing of emperor penguins (Aptenodytes forsteri) using non‐invasively collected guano. Our assay targets short sequences within a conserved exon of the chromodomain helicase DNA binding 1 (CHD1) gene and can therefore be used with a broad range of sample types. We compared the performance of our new primer set in both plucked feathers and guano to the commonly used intron‐based sexing primers (2550F/2718R and P8/P2) and evaluated its sensitivity through a cross‐factorial fragmentation and dilution experiment of synthetic CHD1 templates. We then independently validated the accuracy of our assay in a small subset of feather samples using whole‐genome sequencing (WGS) data. Although P8/P2 was highly effective compared to 2550F/2718R for sex determination in emperor penguins, it was less reliable when used with guano samples. In contrast, the voEP primers consistently yielded higher amplification success and showed greater analytical sensitivity across both feathers and guano. Sequence alignments of CHD1 from multiple penguin species revealed conservation of the primer‐binding sites, suggesting that the newly designed primers can potentially be used with other Spheniscids. Our results demonstrate that the voEP assay is a robust and reliable alternative method for sex identification in penguins and may provide a solution for sexing with lower‐quality genetic samples.
nc1cd8b07b951: Ecological restoration typically relies on locally sourced seed material, yet seed sourcing in many countries is based on broad administrative regions rather than empirical genetic data. Whether these generalized zones reflect biologically meaningful population genomic structure, particularly among co‐occurring species used together in restoration, remains poorly understood, thus limiting genetically informed restoration practices. Here, we use genome‐wide double‐digest RAD sequencing (ddRAD‐seq) to examine spatial population genomic structure in two widespread perennial grassland species commonly used in restoration in Norway: Silene dioica, an obligately outcrossing species with limited seed dispersal, and Achillea millefolium, a polyploid complex characterized by high gene flow and dispersal capacity. Analysis of 17 populations of S. dioica (355 individuals; 19,200 SNPs) and 23 populations of A. millefolium (428 individuals; 21,294 SNPs) across broad latitudinal and climatic gradients in Norway revealed strikingly contrasting patterns of genetic structure. Silene dioica showed moderate spatial structure, significant isolation‐by‐distance, and multiple geographically coherent genetic groups, indicating spatially restricted gene flow and supporting the delineation of multiple seed transfer zones. In contrast, A. millefolium showed weak population differentiation, extensive admixture, and little geographic structuring, but significant isolation‐by‐environment, with annual precipitation emerging as the strongest environmental predictor of genomic differentiation independently of geographic distance, justifying the delineation of three broad genomic zones. Because species‐specific life‐history traits likely contributed to these patterns, a single generalized seed‐sourcing framework can be inadequate even for sympatric species restored together. While the structured genomic patterns in S. dioica support localized seed sourcing, the high connectivity in A. millefolium supports broader transfer zones. Overall, our study highlights the importance of incorporating genomic data into restoration planning by aligning seed transfer distances with species‐specific connectivity to reduce genetic risks and maintain evolutionary potential under environmental change.
nd825c3f58042: The plateau zokor (Eospalax baileyi) is a keystone subterranean rodent species in the alpine meadows of the Qinghai‐Tibet Plateau, and its burrowing and foraging activities exert complex dual effects on grassland ecosystems. Quantifying the relationship between zokor bioturbation and vegetation, ground‐surface and community characteristics, and identifying the ecological management threshold are crucial for sustainable land management. This study selected 21 typical alpine meadow sites along a disturbance gradient on the eastern Qinghai‐Tibet Plateau. We used unmanned aerial vehicle remote‐sensing to extract new mound density as a proxy for relative disturbance intensity and integrated multiple ground‐surveyed indicators into a grassland degradation index, so as to evaluate the association between overall grassland condition and disturbance intensity and to identify the key ecological management threshold. The results showed that vegetation cover and mean height declined linearly and the proportion of bare ground increased linearly with increasing disturbance intensity; community composition exhibited an inverted U‐shaped pattern in species richness and a U‐shaped pattern in the proportion of poisonous plants, whereas aboveground biomass and the proportion of edible forage showed no significant relationship with relative disturbance intensity. Furthermore, a nonlinear relationship was detected between zokor disturbance and the grassland degradation index, and we identified 166 new mounds·ha−1 as the ecological management threshold for plateau zokors; above this threshold, the tendency of grassland condition toward degradation became more pronounced, with surface denudation and deterioration of community composition emerging as the primary constraints on overall grassland condition. This study provides a quantitative basis for shifting alpine meadow management from conventional “pest control” toward threshold‐based adaptive management, and offers a reference for identifying and regulating bioturbation thresholds in other vulnerable ecosystems.
n7cca608b9f30: The evolution and deployment of venom systems in animals have been central to their ecological success, though not without costs. For social bees, venom plays a key role in nest defence; yet for species such as honeybees, the act of stinging generally leads to death. However, for other social bee species such as bumblebees, where stinging is not apparently fatal, it raises the question of what, if any, are the consequences associated with venom usage (envenomation). Here, we investigated proteomic changes to understand consequences that can occur at the molecular level in the venom sac, the primary reservoir for venom storage, of Bombus terrestris workers over a short time‐course post‐envenomation. Our analysis reveals three key findings: (1) envenomation leads to changes in the venom sac proteome, with affected proteins generally reduced in the bumblebee venom sac, suggestive of a molecular cost; (2) quantified reductions of traditional venom‐associated proteins post‐envenomation indicate changes in individual venom protein abundance post‐usage; and (3) recovery period for bumblebee post‐envenomation to return to a non‐envenomation state was required, further indicating a potential cost at the molecular level associated with venom usage. Overall, our findings provide new insights into the molecular consequences of venom usage in bumblebees.
nc984102b7c9c: Coral reefs are among the most biodiverse ecosystems on Earth and rely on endosymbiosis with Symbiodiniaceae, a diverse family of dinoflagellates essential for coral nutrition and which also play an important role in thermal tolerance. Despite their ecological importance, resolving species boundaries within Symbiodiniaceae remains challenging, partly due to limited phylogenetic signal in commonly used genetic markers and the absence of broadly accepted criteria for species delimitation. Refining taxonomic resolution is therefore critical for understanding symbiont diversity, distributions, and evolutionary relationships. In this study, we delimit two closely related Cladocopium species using a meta‐haplotype framework applied to two hypervariable loci—the ITS2 region and the psbA non‐coding region (psbAncr). Slowly evolving markers failed to differentiate Cladocopium proximale (SCF049; described here) from its sister species C. proliferum. In contrast, consistent genetic differences between the two taxa were detected across both hypervariable regions. Together with morphological differences, these results support the recognition of C. proximale and C. proliferum as distinct species. Our results highlight the value of combining multiple hypervariable markers to improve taxonomic accuracy in Symbiodiniaceae, providing a stronger basis for understanding how symbiont diversity and ecological differentiation may influence coral resilience and responses to environmental change. More broadly, closely related Symbiodiniaceae such as these provide important systems for examining speciation processes, including potential ecological differentiation and reproductive compatibility.
n7c83fb2dccc4: The predator–prey relationship between marine mammals and sharks may not be as well defined as originally believed. Both groups can be either predator or prey. In the case of the Pacific sleeper shark, previous studies have documented the sharks predating upon juvenile Steller sea lions and scavenging whale falls, while other studies have reported offshore killer whales predating upon Pacific sleeper shark. Here, we report two observations of likely marine mammal predation upon Pacific sleeper sharks in Southeast Alaska; one of Steller sea lions actively predating upon an approximately 2 m shark; and the other a stranded carcass of a 3 m shark likely predated by killer whales. The observations reported herein are unique in that Steller sea lions have not been documented to predate upon Pacific sleeper sharks, and previous reports of killer whale predation upon Pacific sleeper sharks have been near open ocean passages.
n9ae04f5b701e: Climate change is intensifying fire weather globally, increasing land managers' reliance on prescribed burning to reduce fuel loads and mitigate wildfire risk. Yet the direct effects of prescribed fire on threatened wildlife remain poorly understood, partly because individual‐level data on survival and behaviour during fire events are exceptionally rare. We used VHF telemetry and accelerometry to track the survival, space use and diel activity of nine western ringtail possums (Pseudocheirus occidentalis; ngwayir; eight collared, one uncollared joey)—a Critically Endangered arboreal marsupial widely regarded as highly sensitive to fire—through a low‐ to moderate‐severity prescribed burn at Yalgorup National Park, south‐west Western Australia. All nine animals survived direct fire exposure despite several refuge trees being scorched or structurally damaged. Post‐fire, possums relocated an average of 181 m, but movement distances were unrelated to burn severity and possums showed no selection for unburnt habitat, suggesting limited spatial disruption at the home‐range scale. This may partly reflect the predominantly low‐severity nature of the burn (95.7% of the burnt area). Accelerometry revealed suppressed nocturnal activity during smoke exposure and the fire period, with only partial recovery in the days following the burn, indicating measurable sublethal costs even where direct mortality did not occur. We interpret these behavioural responses as potentially consistent with adaptations shaped by long‐term exposure to frequent, low‐severity fire regimes historically associated with Noongar burning on the Swan Coastal Plain. Although based on a small number of individuals at a single site, and a carefully implemented low‐ to moderate‐severity prescribed burn, our findings provide rare empirical evidence that a critically endangered marsupial can survive prescribed fire. These results have implications for how prescribed burning programs are designed and implemented in the context of evolving fire regimes under climate change.
n10ac24eac913: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Wild animals, particularly large mammalian grazers, can influence ecosystem carbon dynamics and soil carbon sequestration. However, we lack a mechanistic understanding of how wild grazer communities influence soil carbon persistence, specifically in terms of the size of vulnerable free particulate versus more stable occluded particulate and mineral‐associated carbon pools. Resolving this is crucial for predicting how soil carbon is stored long‐term and how grazing management can contribute to soil carbon persistence. We investigated associations between a wild mammalian grazer community and soil carbon persistence in a fire‐prone savanna in South Africa's Hluhluwe‐iMfolozi Park. More specifically, we assessed how variation in grazing (areas grazed at high vs. low intensity) and woody cover (woody‐encroached vs. non‐encroached grassland areas) related to the amount of soil organic carbon (SOC) and pyrogenic organic matter (PyOM, as a proxy for pyrogenic organic carbon) in pools with varying residence times, and how environmental conditions mediated these patterns. In order of increasing residence time, we looked at the free particulate, occluded and mineral‐associated soil carbon pools. Grazing was associated with more SOC in the mineral‐associated pool in fine‐textured soils but less SOC in coarse‐textured soils. In contrast, grazing was associated with more PyOM in the mineral‐associated pool at lower rainfall and in coarser‐textured soils, but less at higher rainfall and in finer‐textured soils. Grazing was also associated with more PyOM in the free particulate pool in finer‐textured soils but less in coarser‐textured soils, and with more PyOM in the occluded pool at low fire frequency but less at high fire frequency. Woody encroachment was consistently associated with less SOC and PyOM in the mineral‐associated pool, with these associations intensifying with higher rainfall (and, for SOC, at higher fire frequency; for PyOM, in finer‐textured soils). In contrast, woody encroachment was associated with more PyOM in the free particulate and occluded pools, although the occluded PyOM associations weakened with higher rainfall and fire frequency. Woody encroachment was associated with less SOC in the free particulate and occluded pools at low rainfall and fire frequency but more SOC at high rainfall and fire frequency. Our study reveals that intense grazing by large wild grazers and woody encroachment are associated with divergent soil carbon persistence outcomes, where the direction and magnitude of these associations are strongly modulated by the environmental context. Therefore, future assessments of large wild grazer impacts on carbon cycling would benefit from considering soil carbon persistence, not just total stocks, together with the environmental context in which these animals occur.
